The randomized Schrödinger solver uses random Schrödinger eigenvalues to solve the Schrödinger equation in multiple dimensions. The method employs random wave vectors whose wave functions are known exactly, allowing for all-dimensional applications with minimal computational cost. The method's generalization ability on high-dimensional problems is evaluated through an expanded dataset. The generalization ability is examined through an expanded dataset, and the method's efficiency is confirmed by comparing its performance to that of gradient-based methods on low-dimensional cases. The method's performance is unaffected by the increase in spatial dimensions.

Research conducted at the Pierre Auger Observatory has identified significant fluctuations in the rate of arrival of the most energetic particles on a large scale, with the variation range substantially wider than 0.2 EeV and also more significant than what was previously predicted for a similar range 5-12 EeV. Data from 10.5 EeV indicating an overall magnitude of 0.7 EeV and a corresponding change in the rate of occurrence when multiplied by the energy to the power of 2.7 and overall magnitude of 0.7 EeV. These observations suggest a substantial change in the distribution and are thought to be associated with ultra-high energy particles originating from specific, localized sources. Two models have been developed for interpreting these observations within the context of limited angular resolution ground-based detectors. Both of these models indicate that the first peak observed in the distribution and ground-based experiments. These models suggest that the overall and ground-based experiments may provide insights into the sources of UHECRs. These models also indicate that the overall and ground-based experiments may provide multiple and distinct sources of UHECRs, with the overall and ground-based experiments may provide multiple and distinct sources of UHECRs, with the overall and ground-based experiments may provide multiple and distinct sources of UHECRs.

This note describes an alternative strategy to derive macroscopic models for incommensurable thin films with periodic microstructures that thin down into a substrate. These films feature two distinct phases with varying elastic properties and a periodic interface between them. Our analysis demonstrates that the previously developed generalized thin film models are not the only possible macroscopic models in this context. Instead, our findings reveal additional models dependent on the way the thin films converge into the substrate. To achieve this, we develop new boundary layers to connect the thin films with the substrate, leveraging a technique called the method of small openings and a related method of reflection.

Our analysis begins with the self-interacting Dirac arena formulated in a flat space and is subsequently applied to the FLRW spacetime using global coordinates. We examine the effects of the FLRW's global structure and the self-interaction on the global properties of the DNAPs.

Training deep learning models for predicting the classification of tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes in H&E-stained histological images is hindered by the scarcity of expertly annotated whole-slide images. To overcome this limitation, we applied federated learning over a collection of expert-annotated digital pathology whole-slide images, resulting in a trained model for individual institutions that retained the expertise of human pathologists. By examining our TIL models trained through both localized and federated approaches, we identified consistent patterns of TIL presence across various tumor types at the cell, tissue, and slide levels. The results demonstrate the capability of federated learning in training high-quality, domain-specific image classification models without requiring the aggregation of digital pathology whole-slide images.

Cavity magnomechanics is a novel field of research that allows for the precise manipulation of spin states, mechanical motion, and light within  magnetic materials. These materials possess unique properties, such as the two-dimensional magnetic effect, which can be exploited to create and amplify quantum phenomena on a macro scale. Our study demonstrates the quantum state fabrication process in cavity magnomechanics involving two-dimensional magnetic materials. We show that two distinct mechanical states can be created, including a coherent state and a Squeezed state. Our research also reveals the possibility of creating light and light-matter entangled states. Furthermore, we found that system parameters can control the purity of the produced quantum states and system phases can be exploited to regulate magnon and phonon populations.

This study presents a novel approach to generating walking gaits for quadrupedal robots without the need for parameters, specifically an evolution-based path generator (EPPG) that creates Gaussian processes to guide motion in a high-dimensional space. By integrating EPPG with reinforcement learning, our method effectively combines its output with a pre-trained model to produce smooth and efficient trajectories for a robot dog. The algorithm's ability to vary trajectory complexity on the fly, adapt to different terrain types, and overcome convergence limitations of traditional trajectory optimization methods makes it a versatile solution for real-world navigation.

We conducted a high-resolution X-ray spectroscopic analysis of the low-luminosity active galactic nucleus in NGC 7213, utilizing observations from XMM-Newton.  The observations revealed low-luminosity broad-line region emission lines and a much lower ionization state than previously documented.  Detailed modeling of the low-luminosity broad-line region revealed super-relativistic speeds of approximately 9,500 km per second.  High-speed outflows have previously been detected in more powerful active galactic nuclei with significantly higher velocities.  Our findings at low Eddington ratios imply a previously unknown mechanism for driving outflows, potentially linked to photon radiation pressure on dust within the accretion disk wind model.  Alternatively, a different driving mechanism entirely may be involved.

A novel control solution for reconfiguring non-linear optimal regulators without a pre-defined model of the plant's dynamics is presented. This on-line model-free method allows for the recovery of plant controllability and optimizes the performance of the reconfigured regulator. It combines a non-linear optimal regulator with a data-driven algorithm in two distinct stages: initially, the non-linear optimal regulator is tuned using reinforcement learning without model identification; subsequently, a reinforcement learning variant based on state similarity clusters the system's operating modes and refines the regulator's parameters based on this information. This innovative approach is demonstrated on a test-bed motor drive with intentional sensor failures.

Ca' Manger's Cluster Tonantzintla 2 is located in the Milky Way's disk's southern hemisphere and contains 17 members with 10 stars with the CAPOS dataset and external datasets supplementing the sample to 17 stellar systems. Effective land resource management relies on accurate, timely data from the Earth's surface to address issues like food security and disaster prevention. However, the task of extracting such data is labor-intensive and requires significant human effort. This paper proposes a new AI framework, EarthNets, to automate the data annotation process for resource classification. By combining various data sources, including high-resolution maps, we demonstrate the potential for efficiently training accurate models for land use classification. Our results show that the models derived from our framework achieve state-of-the-art performance, reducing the required data by a factor of 10 without significantly impacting accuracy. Additionally, we significantly improved the quality of data by retraining the models to better align with the original training data. Our framework utilizes publicly available data, and it can serve as a starting point for efficient Earth resource monitoring.

We systematically study the dynamics of active nematic films in the thick membrane regime. Through dimensional analysis, we identify the primary factors governing this system's behavior. We use dynamic renormalization group analysis to examine the implications of wave-like disturbances and instability in the order parameter and show how they lead to a renormalized order parameter equation. We also study the stability of 2D vortices within the context of this order parameter equation. We use this analysis to create a parameter space diagram that outlines distinct dynamics regimes. We conclude by discussing possible extensions to these thin films in the context of active gel theory.

In the era of data-driven business, ensuring the reliability of online services and systems becomes increasingly vital for sustaining business success. This necessity drives the need for effective methods that can detect irregularities in data streams in real-time. This research focuses on developing a reliable method to spot unusual patterns within a segment of data streams without pre-defined norms. This method utilizes a dynamic division technique to break the data into segments and employs the weighted sum of squared errors (WSS) to assess the fit of a linear regression model to each segment. Subsequently, segments with significantly higher WSS values are further analyzed to isolate unusual data points. The approach demonstrated the ability to accurately detect irregularities and minimize false positives on both real-world and engineered data streams. Additionally, the method exhibits a low computational cost, making it suitable for real-time implementation.

Pion vector shape factors have been thoroughly investigated and computed using various methods to aid in experimental analyses at LAB and other facilities, such as PANDA. These shape factors have played a critical role in analyzing pion production processes in exclusive reactions. Our team performed detailed studies, including total and differential cross sections, to evaluate their impact on the recent measurement of the muon anomalous magnetic moment. Specific considerations involved the pion vector form factor's effect on two-photon pion production, which can significantly influence experimental outcomes.

New techniques in deep learning have led to the development of innovative models for text and code tasks, yet their ability to process code globally remains limited.
In this paper, we explore the problem of creating a universal representation for code, relevant to both programmers and machine, and its applications in addressing off-text tasks.
We conduct a comprehensive evaluation of code representation techniques across multiple programming languages, revealing the shortcomings of existing text-based approaches and the limited performance of current deep learning models for code Off-text problems.
We also identify key barriers to the effective machine processing of code Off-text data, and propose a list of research challenges that could be tackled in order to advance this field.

Our understanding of how galaxies form and evolve is hindered by the lack of a clear theoretical framework that links the mass of galaxies to their morphology. Recent studies have attempted to fill this gap by examining current galaxy structures, but their findings are inconclusive due to the complexity of these forms. A new study employs an innovative statistical method to examine the connection between the masses of galaxies in different structures, discovering that certain morphology-dependent relationships hold true when accounting for dynamics. The results show that early-type galaxies have a stronger relationship with their surrounding dark matter halos than late-type galaxies, confirming previous findings and providing insight into the mechanisms of galaxy formation. Moreover, a novel observation reveals that late-type galaxies in densely clustered environments have a stronger relationship with their surrounding dark matter halos than those in less dense environments, suggesting that environmental factors play a significant role in the formation of this type of galaxy. The study's approach provides a new perspective on galaxy morphology and its connection with dark matter halos, offering a foundation for future research into the mechanisms of galaxy formation and the evolution of galaxy structures.

Historically, atmospheric turbulence has been considered detrimental to astronomical observation quality, reducing the clarity of astronomical images. The variability in starlight intensity, however, has been utilized to aerosol properties in the absence of specialized weather instruments. The Differential, Astrometric, Differential, Aperture, Photometry (DDAP) method effectively separates astrophysical signals, allowing for the precise evaluation of aerosol transmission and optical turbulence. The application of the DDAP technique to multiple stars with varying colors and magnitudes enables the distillation of intrinsic astrophysical variability, facilitating the creation of high-resolution vertical profiles of aerosol distribution. The comparison of measurements with numerical models or numerical weather models can verify the accuracy of derived data and suggest potential transport mechanisms, such as convective currents. The application of the DDAP method in various weather conditions offers a continuous, high-resolution monitoring system, serving as a complementary tool to existing meteorological instruments and providing input for numerical models.

The Generalized Graphical Lasso (GGL) problem is an extension of the Graphical Lasso (GL) problem, incorporating additional constraints on edge weights to accommodate limited data scenarios. To address this challenge, two novel methods have been developed, which were integrated into the GGLasso Python library. This library provides a user-friendly interface for solving the GGL problem, as well as efficient implementations of the proposed methods, and was released under a permissive license to support reproducible research in the statistical community.

The two prevailing theories explaining atmospheric loss in planetary planets are disk evaporation and disk breeze models. Despite various findings from observations of young stellar systems by different instruments, determining the extent of atmospheric loss in these models remains a challenge. With a focus on the protoplanetary disk around the very low mass TWA1 (also known as 2M1237) star, our research utilizes high-frequency radio observations from the Common Astronomy Imaging Mobile Experiment (CAMEX-5) experiment to atmospheric loss rates. Using a modified version of the radiative transfer code DALI, we determined radio emissions of thermal dust at 1.3 mm within the top few hundred micron layers of the disk. Our findings reveal a mass loss rate of approximately $4.8\times 10^{-14}M_{\odot}$/yr. Further analysis of model dependencies showed that a dust density factor of $10^4$ is suitable within the top few micron layers of the photoevaporation model. However, a different type of modification within the magnetic model produced a similar match. Moreover, a mass loss rate of $10^{-13}M_{\odot}$/yr could be accommodated within the magnetic model without altering its modification factor. Ultimately, our research suggests that a photoevaporation model best explains the radio emissions of the low mass TWA1 star.

The detection of unsegmented speech involves identifying both the presence of speech and its division into individual sounds. For speech recognition systems, it's essential to first separate the speech from background noise and then break it down into phonetic units. Current methods that rely on established databases are ineffective for spoken languages that have not been included in the training data. A proposed approach tackles these challenges simultaneously by using a data-driven, unsupervised method based on the statistics of speech units. This method achieves a high accuracy in separating speech from noise and splitting the speech into individual sounds without requiring manual labeling. Additionally, the system uses the duration of speech segments to refine its estimates of the tone in each segment, which in turn improves the accuracy of speech sound identification. As a result, the system outperforms a traditional baseline that uses Gaussian mixture models for speech recognition.

We introduce a new method, dynamically weighted inertial forward-backward algorithm, that incorporates the forward-backward algorithm with Yoshimoto's inertial algorithm. This algorithm draws on the principles of Euler integrators to ensure feasibility within the constraints of the problem, while leveraging the Tikhonov regularization inherent in the algorithm to ensure convergence to a solution of the problem. This approach targets an expansive class of nonexpansive monotone inclusions that have eluded conventional forward-backward methods due to the absence of strict monotonicity or expansive properties. Moreover, we integrate the principles of Fejer monotonicity and the Loewitt-Ornstein Theorem to ensure that the algorithm's iterations remain bounded and converge strongly as they approach a solution of the problem. Moreover, under certain circumstances, we establish local superlinear convergence as an experiment demonstrates the efficacy of the newly developed algorithm.

This research investigates loop corrections to the Higgs boson mass in a next-to-minimal supersymmetric standard model, combined with a reverse seesaw model for generating neutrino masses. By incorporating right-handed neutrinos into the model, the radiative corrections to the Higgs mass potential are evaluated at the one-loop level. In addition, the model is analyzed within the context of the Feynman arboretum framework, and the status of neutrino data and Higgs potential findings is discussed.

Using neural networks, many real-world problems can be solved, and optimizing their architecture significantly impacts their performance and resource efficiency. In aerospace engineering, predicting fluid flow patterns is also crucial and can be achieved through neural networks, specifically through the use of lattice Boltzmann lattice Boltzmann methods. This research introduces a novel neural network design approach based on property-directed synthesis and demonstrates its effectiveness in optimizing the performance of simulating fluid dynamics through neural networks. The optimization process using neural networks, specifically through the optimization of the LSTM architecture, resulted in a 10-fold improvement over traditional methods. Furthermore, we explored the transferability of these results to other problems, including image classification and optimization of the MLP architecture, with positive outcomes indicating further potential for advancement.

In the future of wireless communication, millimeter wave (mmWave) technology is considered a crucial component, particularly in multi-group broadcasting scenarios. The complexity of these scenarios arises from the substantial computational requirements necessitated by multi-carrier systems, which comprise a significant number of frequency subcarriers. The primary algorithm used for multi-carrier systems, the inverse fast Fourier transform (IFFT), has a time complexity that impacts the overall system efficiency. The proposed solution involves a new hybrid encoding algorithm designed to reduce the complexity, leveraging a specific property observed in multi-group broadcasting mmWave systems, namely reduced inter-carrier interference resulting from the identical data transmission of multiple subcarriers to various groups. By exploiting this characteristic, the complexity of the encoding process can be diminished from O(NlogN) to O(NlogG), where 'N' represents the total number of subcarriers, and 'G' signifies the number of groups. The feasibility and performance of this innovative hybrid encoding approach are successfully demonstrated through numerical simulations.

Federated Learning (FL) communication efficiency is a critical issue in cross-device machine learning. This work addresses this challenge by introducing a new method, communication-effective federated learning (CEFL), which reduces communication overhead. Communication efficiency is enhanced by integrating knowledge distillation and quantization. Specifically, a light-weight student model is trained and its parameters are then compacted for efficient transmission. This reduces transmitted data size by approximately two times. We propose two effective schemes, average quantization and mixed quantization, to ensure accurate gradient updates despite compression. These results demonstrate that communication effective federated learning achieves comparable performance and accuracy to state-of-the-art while significantly reducing communication costs by up to two times.

Decentralized data retrieval in Content-Centric Networks (CCN) is the primary objective, but due to limited storage capacity and unreliable connectivity, it is often unattainable. To overcome this obstacle, we suggest integrating the NDN data plane with the Google OR-Tools optimization tool. Using this tool, we optimize Content-Caching Networks (CNs) to optimize both the content distribution strategy and routing protocols. Furthermore, we introduce a new concept of dynamic store-and-forward forwarding in CNs to achieve optimal performance, and to facilitate this, we define ideal dynamic coordination, where store-and-forward operations are perfectly synchronized. To achieve this coherence, we employ the shortest path tree and introduce an efficient content distribution strategy based on it. Moreover, we define a set of necessary conditions for coherent content caching and present an overview of our work within the Context-Centric Environment (CEE).

The long-beam equation on a graph, consisting of finitely many edges, near a stationary state on a star-forming graph, exhibits unique properties. Specifically, this beam equation possesses only finitely many vibrational modes, which vary based on the angles at junctions on the star-forming graph. Conversely, continuous spectra emerge from vertices with angles of $2\pi$. For cases where this beam equation is conservative, we observe that all local and quasi-local stability outcomes from previous studies extend to the star-forming graph. However, damping on one edge leads to uniform stability outcomes, which depend on the presence of a specific frequencyless mode, particularly at the junction edge. When this mode absent, damping yields all frequencies of local decay outcomes, otherwise, only a given rate of local decay outcomes, which depends on the supremum frequency of the residual frequencies, which in turn depends on the junction angular frequency.

To address the long-standing issue of chiral symmetry breaking in quark matter, an explicit breaking of this symmetry is integrated into the quark-meson model with two flavors of quarks. The presence of this symmetry breaking is found to eliminate the phase transition and instead result in a series of distinct regions separated by the phase boundary. Within these regions, three types of complex structures emerge: T-type, W-type, and S-type patterns, each displaying unique morphological characteristics. During the formation of these structures, both spinodal decomposition and growth processes are observed, while the overall behavior exhibits dependence on the magnitude of this symmetry-breaking parameter.

Recent theoretical predictions have suggested the existence of a new class of topological insulators with Tl framework - MTl4Te3 (where MTl4Te3 forms a tetrahedron). The purpose of this study is to verify the predicted properties through specific calculations. The researchers utilized ab-initio calculations to analyze the predicted characteristics of the material. The outcomes of the study showed that the system exhibits specific atomic arrangements, electronic band gaps of approximately 0.25 eV, topological properties and effective mass values of around 0.45 for both conduction and valence bands, which are in excellent agreement with the predicted values. Additionally, the researchers found that the system exhibits specific temperature-dependent effective mass values due to electron-phonon coupling interactions and possesses carrier effective masses lower than that of graphene. The phase stability of the materials was confirmed via Gibbs free energy and phase stability studies and these results indicated that the materials exhibit specific optical properties and excellent Verwey mobility.

Achieving optimal design and control often relies on parameter optimization, particularly for complex systems characterized by high computational costs and the existence of Pareto-optimal solutions. In such cases, defining utility functions that reflect the preferences of decision-makers is crucial for narrowing down the range of optimal objectives. However, deriving these utility functions directly from information from decision makers is often an arduous process. To overcome this challenge, we propose an utility function learning method that enables the efficient discovery of preferred decision maker utilities, even with a limited set of evaluations. By bypassing direct elicitations and instead learning utility functions from a limited number of parameter optimizations informed by prior information, we demonstrate in two test cases that our approach outperforms traditional methods. To further accelerate the learning process and reduce the number of required evaluations, we integrate a Kriging-based surrogate with multi-objective optimization, employing the Shapley effect to efficiently locate Pareto-optimal solutions.

As more organizations rely on reinforcement learning, it becomes crucial to safeguard these systems from malicious attacks. Recent studies have focused on developing blackbox adversarial examples in reinforcement learning environments, but these approaches often require substantial interaction with the target, making the attack process cumbersome. Our proposed blackbox attack approach, however, significantly reduces the number of interactions needed to generate adversarial examples by exploiting information about the adversary's location within the environment. Although this method assumes some level of knowledge about the adversary's position, it offers a more efficient alternative to blackbox attack techniques that do not require such information. Our findings also reveal that even blackbox attack methods which assume no environment information can still create successful adversarial examples by using sensitive reward functions as a training tool.

Properties of materials at the atomic level which incorporate both topological characteristics and their crystalline symmetries show exceptional performance when combined. Investigations into two-dimensional atomic arrangements like the hexagonal honeycomb structure have led to a significant breakthrough in understanding the characteristics of graphene, specifically through its exceptional electronic properties. When considering the symmetries of this structure, the space group 193 (which combines its translational properties with those of its point group) offers unique possibilities. In this context, this study examines a hexagonal supercell based on the p4mm symmetry, which contains two distinct honeycomb lattices. By applying tight-binding models to this structure, it's found that Dirac points can be created within the first Brillouin zone, exhibiting high degeneracy. These adjustable Dirac points exhibit high linear dispersion which becomes quantifiable at specific high symmetry points in the Brillouin zone. Various methods are used to verify the linear dispersion at these points including calculation of the zone's geometry using the formula $\mathbf{B}=\frac{2\pi}{S}$. Results also indicate that the characteristics of these Dirac points can be quantified through the formula $\mathcal{C}_4$ which represents four-fold rotation symmetry. These results have significant implications for understanding material design where the exceptional properties of these materials can be exploited in advanced applications.

The goal of risk-averse reinforcement learning (RL) in non-stationary environments is to develop policies that balance expected rewards and risk, whereas risk-averse RL in stationary environments primarily focuses on optimizing this balance. This study aims to study risk-averse RL in non-stationary environments under the framework of dynamic regret, where the regret of a policy is defined as the difference between its expected rewards and the rewards of the optimal policy over a time period. A key challenge is that the optimal policy is not always identifiable due to the potential existence of multiple non-stationary optimal time intervals. However, we show that the identification of at least one non-stationary optimal interval is sufficient to achieve near-optimal dynamic regret. Specifically, we find that the regret upper bound increases as the complexity of the underlying problem, the variance of the optimal policy, and the complexity of the underlying problem increase, while the bound decreases as the policy's exploration rate and the degree of policy stability increase. Notably, our analysis reveals that achieving near-optimal dynamic regret does not require identifying the entire optimal policy, but rather the identification of just one non-stationary optimal interval is sufficient. Another significant issue is the trade-off between theoretical guarantees and practical performance in real-world applications. Typically, the exploration design is set uniformly to simplify the analysis and interpretation of the results. However, we argue that non-uniform exploration design can improve the environment's stability and the efficiency of policy learning, thus reducing the exploration rate

The development of adaptive problem tracking systems is a significant area of study in computer science. These systems are used by software developers to monitor the progress of their projects, including the creation of software and the maintenance of existing applications. The effectiveness of these systems is measured by their ability to adapt to the evolving needs of individual teams, thereby enhancing their productivity. The existing research relies heavily on data collected from public Jira repositories. These repositories contain information about the tracking of problems and their resolution methods used by successful teams. However, there is a significant gap in research due to a lack of readily available datasets for analysis. To address this issue, a new research study proposes the creation of an alternate dataset by combining and reorganizing data from multiple public Jira repositories. This new dataset can be utilized for statistical analysis and comparison with the existing tracking data. In order to prevent unnecessary repetition, the research study aims to provide an in-depth analysis of the characteristics of this proposed dataset.

The growing importance of datasets spread across multiple devices in the technology sector drives the need for advanced Machine Learning that can function efficiently within stringent time constraints. However, conventional Distributed Machine Learning approaches are often impractical due to device failures, leading to suboptimal performance, especially for linear models, which show only marginal improvements over centralized models. This paper introduces a novel non-linear distribution function for weight averaging in Distributed Machine Learning, which incorporates the concept of a distribution of complex numbers. This approach offers time-invariant performance in Distributed Linear Model learning, and the performance gap between central and edge computation can be closed by selecting an appropriate aggregation function, according to the paper's analysis.

We've developed an innovative approach utilizing a specialized grating that enables the creation of numerous arrays of trapped atoms within an integrated system. A key component is the use of coupled waveguides that trap and stabilize atoms via a combination of radial and axial confinement. Our proposed design allows for efficient single-atom identification within a trap array by employing a diffusion process that releases atoms into a detection zone. Additionally, we've designed a system that enables the trapping, manipulation, and reading out of individual atoms in a specific subset of the trapped atoms using microwaves and focused reading beams. Our integrated approach offers significant advantages for future quantum information applications.

Let the monoid of finite words, denoted as $\Lambda^*$, be based on a partially ordered set of letters $\Lambda$ and specifically, a distributive lattice. We present a method to compute the MacNeille completion of $\Lambda^*$ purely through the use of its original alphabet. This completion is then shown to be homeomorphic to the Kleene monoid of the Dushnik-Blassler-Turanski order derived from $\Lambda$. Furthermore, the method allows for the computation of key lattice structures within the completion from the original algebraic operations on $\Lambda^*$. Lastly, our approach yields a homeomorphism between the Schützenberger order on the Kleene monoid and a specific order completion of the free monoid $\Lambda^*$.

To create synthetic elements, we suggest a method that starts with period
and atomic weight as basic variables, using linear regression to determine the formation of compound atomic weights. A formation reaction is set up for every polymerelement with a target polymeresymbol, and the elements within it are selected using a suitable selection criterion. An constraint is added to ensure that no elements are repeated, and it becomes possible to derive new formation reactions using this revised setup. Ultimately, this new polymerelement derivation technique is applied to develop new polymerelements with atomic weights exceeding 118.

In the field of optimal control, two primary categories of solution methods, known as indirect and direct approaches, are utilized to address biomedicine and healthcare challenges. Indirect and direct architectures provide valuable insights but may not fully capture the dynamics of personalized medical treatments. To address this limitation, we introduce the concept of direct transcription for dynamic enhancement, a new framework that integrates personalization and adaptability to produce highly precise predictions and treatment plans. Through a case study involving the COVID-19 pandemic, we illustrate the effectiveness of the new architecture in addressing the dynamics of treatments under changing conditions. Our research specifically focuses on radiobiology and radiotherapy radio-planning but has wide-ranging applications in the planning of complex medical treatments and public health policy development.

Let $f$ be a rational function with degree more than one over the complex numbers, which when iterated repeatedly always results in a rational function, is not a Lattimore map of level two, and when specialized results in transcendental values produces a transcendental outcome. If we denote the set of preimages of critical points as $I_f$, and the set containing both critical points and one additional point as $W_f$, then the intersection of the two sets, $I_f \cap W_f$, is not an empty set. Our goal is to demonstrate that the maximum order of an element in the Galois group of the field extended by the $n$-th iterate of $f$ and the set of preimages of critical points, for any positive integer $n$, is limited and does not depend on $n$. Additionally, the field of rational functions over the complex numbers, when specialized to any transcendental value, is not equal to the field of rational functions over the complex numbers with the set of preimages of critical points.

In the context of linear regression, particularly in high-dimensional settings where variance is unknown, this work investigates a novel predictive framework utilizing characteristics derived from one-step estimators. These characteristics serve as a foundation for constructing empirical priors in Bayesian models, enabling us to examine their performance in complex scenarios with numerous variables and sample sizes using the Lasso and its variants. Our findings reveal that such empirical priors produce Bayesian estimators with approximate oracle performance, yielding near-minimal prediction errors and logarithmic loss risks, thus outperforming traditional methods like the Lasso in terms of risk convergence. Moreover, we investigate the impact on predictive performance when the empirical priors involve random variables correlated with the model uncertainty.

Assessing the energy efficiency of machining centers is a critical step in improving their performance and reducing overall energy consumption. Traditional voltage, current, and power measurements have limitations in providing meaningful insights into energy usage. To overcome this, a Bayesian approach was employed to select the most relevant energy monitoring parameters and reduce noise from less significant variables. The probability of each parameter was evaluated and the top contributing variables were retained. Following this analysis, a genetic algorithm optimized the remaining data for better representation of the facility's energy consumption. The results indicated that only two variables from the initial dataset contributed over 95% to the energy consumption and power. Our methodology successfully compressed over 90% of the data without losing valuable information. The optimized energy monitors enabled the control system to efficiently regulate energy consumption during automated machining operations, leading to over a 20% reduction in energy usage. The proposed method can be further applied to other systems for effective energy management.

The spectral dimension of a random walk on a countable connected graph is determined by the exponent in which the return probability of the walk, starting at a given vertex, decreases with time. Theorem 1 establishes that under the condition of a regular and conformal measure, the spectral dimension can be expressed in terms of the fractal dimension associated with this measure and its associated exponent. This generalizes a previous result in a specific case where the exponent is zero. Furthermore, Theorem 2 proves that for graphs satisfying a certain growth condition with respect to this measure, the fractal dimension is equal to the spectral dimension. Both findings are applicable to a wide range of group graphs.

A significant issue in simulations of heavy-quark decay concerns the incorporation of the $\eta_c$ and $\eta_Q$ states, and we suggest implementing an in-depth mixing model in such calculations. Currently, many analyses exclude the influence of $\eta_c$ and $\eta_Q$ and instead utilize an approximate "effective" mass for these particles, often based on the lighter of the two masses. This approach neglects their individual contributions. To address these concerns, a new method utilizing the $\eta_c$-mass, the $\eta_Q$-mass, and additional parameters derived from experimental data is presented to estimate the actual hadronic decay product mass. We apply this approach to the heavy-quark decay of $J/\psi$ into a photon and an unknown hadronic particle to obtain a parameterized form of the decay spectrum. Further analysis of the resulting spectrum reveals a notable discrepancy with the experimental data, suggesting that the nature of the hadronic component requires additional consideration.

The goal of this study is to obtain empirical evidence for the presence of
complex, recurring elements in genuine signature examples from various
individuals to support the use of this type of data in signature-based access
control systems. The findings presented in this paper confirm the presence of
three essential characteristics - uniqueness, intricacy, and reproducibility -
of online signature templates. The research specifically focuses on fingerprinting
live individuals as they sign their names, capturing both movement and position,
while analyzing a diverse sample size of 250 online signatures from 50 different
individuals, with each person signing 5 times per fingerprint to ensure accuracy
and reliability. The results indicate that the average F-score for signature
repeatability across all captured fingerprints and instances, is approximately 0.36,
and the Cauchy-Schwarz distance metric for signature complexity averages around 0.03.
The research demonstrates that the aforementioned characteristics are both
statistically and practically significant, and thus provides a solid foundation
for using the captured fingerprint information to verify an individual's identity
through their signature.

We investigate the four-derivative superpotential in N=6 four-dimensional string models constructed using the asymmetric orbifold method. As part of our study, we examine the six-derivative potential in one particular model to gauge its magnitude relative to the four-derivative term. Our findings reveal a substantial lower limit for this ratio, estimated at 0.008. Moreover, we observe that the superpotential's coefficient adheres to the expected structure predicted by Cudell and Kounnas in 1991. Notably, in certain models, the superpotential can be tuned and potentially eliminated entirely.

Our research employs higher-order associativity to examine the complex relationships between spin patterns within patterns containing a fixed number of bits of information. Utilizing the Solovay-Kitaev algorithm, our results demonstrate that the spin patterns within our test cases can be categorized into a hierarchical structure. This hierarchical organization becomes more pronounced at deeper levels of the hierarchy when the size of the circuit increases. Furthermore, this hierarchical structure exhibits distinct correlations with various properties, including circuit efficiency, depth, and the distribution of leaf nodes. Notably, a previously observed phenomenon, where low-hierarchy spin patterns exhibit improved resilience to noise when placed at the base levels of the tree, is replicated with our algorithm. This reinforces the validity of our analytical approach.

One critical test for theories about the universe's elemental composition is whether nitrogen can be formed through nuclear reactions. Past research has established that under specific conditions, the amount of 4He is limited to a maximum value and that certain models cannot explain high ratios of 3He without significantly increasing 4He beyond its observed levels. Our study finds similar constraints apply to nitrogen, with specific 15O and 13O isotopes being key factors. As nitrogen models require a specific ratio of 3He to 4He, our data suggests 15O must be enhanced by a factor of at least 100 or the 3He/4He ratio must reach a specific, higher level. Our findings also reveal that a certain type of baryon transformation would increase the ratio of 3He to 4He in line with nitrogen models.

Multilingual individuals who communicate in more than one language are becoming increasingly prevalent on social media platforms, particularly in countries where English and a local language are dominant. Despite the growth in multilingual interactions, especially between English and other languages, research in code-mixing NLP has not received as much attention as it deserves. This paper offers an in-depth examination of English-Indian Language code-mixing from the perspective of NLP researchers, examining both language barriers to developing effective RNLP systems and opportunities that arise, such as the need for better linguistic tools and algorithms.

Biomedical research is inherently interdisciplinary and can be viewed through the lens of diverse data types that are both structured and unstructured.  Graphs serve as a fundamental framework for representing and analyzing such data, yet their representation has been overlooked in the progress of biomedical artificial intelligence despite advances in deep learning capabilities.  This course aims to bridge this knowledge gap by exploring graph modeling in biomedical research through the lens of fundamental concepts and contemporary methods.  The course will delve into diverse topics including model learning from diverse graph data, different biomedical graph model types, integrating graph neural networks and deep learning, and refining model validation and interpretation.  A particular emphasis will be placed on the significance of explainable and safe model development in the context of biomedical applications where the underlying process is complex and inconstant.  The course will also showcase case studies drawing from diverse fields such as epidemiology, pharmacology, and medicine to underscore the diversity of graph modeling and its broad relevance in biomedical research.

Recent measurements of enhanced white dwarf cooling rates imply that certain types of subatomic particles, specifically those that could be a candidate for dark matter, must have a minimum mass. This has significant implications if dark matter interacts with ordinary matter through the weak force. In this context, we have re-evaluated the constraints that these enhanced cooling rates place on the properties of the particles in two theoretical models, one that swaps left and right sides under the weak interaction, with a specific right-side counterpart, and another where dark matter interacts with specific particles under a baryon-based property. We have determined that these constraints are significantly weakened by the requirements of neutron star composition and the absence of certain signals from star formation processes in the early universe, causing them to become insignificant in these two models.

Advances in machine learning have led to the creation of content-based privacy systems that protect user data. However, research indicates that such systems are often ineffective, as they rely on a universal security standard for all image classes, ignoring their varying risk levels. This study proposes GraphPrivacy, a content-based privacy filter based on graph neural networks (GNNs), which is capable of identifying high-risk image classes and applying an appropriate security level to each. Following the extraction of features from graph neural network content, GraphPrivacy uses a dual-branch model to predict class labels and assess the class's risk level. By sharing hidden layers, the system shares knowledge across components and improves performance. When integrated with existing image security systems, such as Yolo, performance tests have showcased an 8% enhancement in accuracy and a 14% reduction in processing time.

This paper explores the prospects of further developing Purity as a concealing property. It introduces four models that reflect different levels of Purity's potential, and and demonstrates why Purity is included in a specific subset of these models, while excluding the others. Additionally, the paper investigates the relationships between the remaining models, and their Concealing Property Property (CPP) status is determined to be independent of one another.

This study compares the fragmentation behaviors of light-quark and gluon jets within proton-proton and lead-lead collisions at the LHC. Using a simulated tag-trig method, we isolate gluon and quark jets by leveraging the event shape property, namely, wide and narrow jet jettiness, in $p$-Pb and Pb+Pb collisions at 5.02 and 9.1 TeV, with selected gluon and quark jets exhibiting similar bulk properties. The measurements focus on the $dN^{j}/d\eta_{\rm hit}$ distribution of track hits inside jets and the charged-particle fragmentation functions for both $p$+$p$ and Pb+Pb at various analysis stages. The results reveal that the medium-induced fragmentation in Pb+Pb differs for gluon and quark jets. The results also reveal that gluon jets fragment more rapidly than quark jets regardless of the center-of-mass energy. The findings are consistent with the expectations from the color charge difference between gluon and quark jets.

The CP2K program package, often seen as an exemplar of efficient open-source software, finds widespread application in cutting-edge computational research across various fields including chemistry and physics. With a prominent role in leading ab-initio modeling techniques such as density functional theory and quantum dynamics, efficient in-memory and disk data handling plays a crucial role in its success. This work details the advancements made in the recent version of the package that facilitate large-scale computing on the most advanced supercomputers, encompassing innovations in the fully-exact ab-initio/MD solver that leverages GPU technology and advanced memory structures. Furthermore, we discuss strategies employed to maximize the performance of the package on the latest CPU and GPU architectures by incorporating the latest communication structures and pinned memory structures. Our findings indicate that the package has achieved remarkable efficiencies with scales of up to 10 million CPU cores and 500 PB of RAM.

The most recent solar flare "Reuven" X-ray Imager's solar module observed the F4.7 flare on May 13, 2021, as it underwent two significant phases: impulsive and decaying. Contrary to expectations, the coronal emission persisted at a low level during the impulsive phase, and the brightest soft X-rays appeared during the flare's decay. Following this, the coronal emission continued at a reduced intensity for over 20 minutes, and the flare's high-energy components were finally detected with RXITi for the first time during this event, appearing approximately 8 minutes after the peak. Observations from RXITi indicate a significant difference in emission characteristics between impulsive and decaying phases, and they also demonstrate how these components and X-rays vary over time. Furthermore, RXITi's data allow us to estimate key parameters, including electron temperatures, densities, and sizes of the coronal region, which underwent the event. Lastly, RXITi's data suggest a correlation between the coronal region's size and its minimum electron density as a function of temperature.

Predicting social influence in various fields like time-series data is essential but extremely difficult. This difficulty stems from the complex interplay between different features that are often represented as graph data. Recent advancements in Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have shown great promise in resolving this issue, enabling accurate predictions. Nevertheless, standard GNNs have limitations in handling time-series data augmentation, which is crucial to prevent overfitting. This paper presents a breakthrough by adapting two key techniques, train and test duration augmentation from traditional machine learning to GNNs, effectively addressing the problem. The proposed methods serve as vital tools to enhance the model's generalization capability and improve predictions. The results indicate that these techniques yield substantial accuracy boosts when paired with GNNs, specifically showing notable gains in predicting time-series data with spatial dependencies. The findings are validated through experiments on synthetic and real-world data sets.

The dimension of the CFT's operator algebra, known as the dimension of the conformal bootstrap, is best understood through a connection to integrable mechanics. Utilizing the Euler-Arnold equations, which describe the motion of a Lie algebra, we establish a method to identify specific unitary representations of the conformal group in two CFTs: $\mathcal{N}=4$ superconformal symmetry in four-dimensional spacetime and two-dimensional conformal symmetry. By applying this method, we derive lower bounds on the dimension of the CFT's operator spectrum for specific theories, including a well-known theory called the critical Ising model, achieving precision within 1% of the current best estimates obtained through machine learning and an extension of bootstrap methods. Furthermore, we find that our construction of the CFT's conformal primary operators through conformal bootstrap guarantees their independence from one another.

This research focuses on deriving the optimal estimator for a system's state based on noisy position measurements from multiple reference points. While least squares estimation is commonly used in engineering and the life sciences, it often fails in cases where measurement errors are non-random or systems are geometrically complex. Our study resolves these limitations by employing a geometric approach to linearization, enabling the application of least squares methods to complex systems. A novel algorithm, complete least squares, is proposed as a comprehensive solution to ordinary least squares limitations, featuring closed-form solutions for systems with linear and complex geometric constraints. Additionally, our work includes a statistical analysis of estimation bias and covariance, along with the development of an optimality criterion. This criterion serves not only for evaluating the optimality of estimates but also for simplifying and solving complex optimization problems. We demonstrate the broad applicability of our approach by applying it to the flow velocity optimization problem.

Researchers are investigating the hidden sector, which might have interacted with the standard model, within the early universe's high-temperature environment.  A hypothetical dark photon could be the long-sought hidden sector mediator.  Research suggests that, in the beginning, the dark photon dark sector might have been at a lower temperature compared to the standard model's plasma.  However, if the dark photon's coupling to the standard model increases sufficiently, thermal equilibrium could be reached, leading to a split-universe with co-existing, separate thermal equilibriums.  A research team analyzed dark photon dark sector and standard model thermal equilibriums within the early universe, particularly focusing on their phase transitions.  Their research revealed that the standard model and the dark photon's couplings could be compatible within the early universe, but at a temperature of approximately 260 GeV due to the QCD transition, the dark photon's coupling constant reaches its peak value of 0.01.  Furthermore, the researchers observed that within the hypothetical dark photon dark sector, a thermal phase transition might have occurred, which could happen at a temperature of around 5 MeV, but only under specific conditions, specifically when the dark photon's mass is around 5 eV.  However, if this phase transition were to happen, it would likely decouple the dark photon from the standard model, rendering their combined thermal equilibrium impossible, thus rendering the proposed thermal equilibrium scenario viable only within a narrow parameter range. A comprehensive search for simultaneously charged W bosons generated through weak forces has been conducted using and combining datasets from proton-proton collisions at a high energy of 13 TeV. The experimental search was conducted using a advanced CMS detector at the CERN LHC facility. The quantities of events exceeding normal expectations were discovered in numerous categories corresponding to various ranges of total energy and momentum in the final state containing two same-sign W bosons, which occurred at a confidence level of 95% which sets an upper limit of 0.34 events per picobarn per year cross section at a confidence level of 95% which is essential in understanding the fundamental particle interactions at a fine level of granularity.

This research introduces an innovative technique for enhancing color information in monochromatic video feeds from different cameras. Our approach involves training a cross-camera mapping network that can accurately reproduce the output of another camera using raw image data. However, since only grayscale images are available, we've developed a method to directly predict color images from monochromatic input. A camera-specific monochromatic to color dataset was created for this purpose, consisting of image sequences from eight Color CCTV cameras covering seven distinct color spaces. The dataset includes downsampled and black-and-white versions for training and evaluating the deep learning models. Notably, the proposed method outperforms existing color video generation techniques in terms of camera invariance and image quality.

A new analysis of the $\Lambda$CDM cosmological model is conducted by reevaluating constraints on curvature based on latest Planck data and incorporating datasets of large-scale structure to replace earlier results that relied on lesser-quality Cosmic Microwave Radiation measurements. Specifically, analyses of Euclid's lensing data simulation, Baryon Acoustic Oscillations, and the Dark Energy Survey's weak lensing data show an abundance of evidence for a curved universe in analysis of the curvature parameter $\sigma_m^2$. By combining these datasets, researchers have determined that the value of $\sigma_m^2$ equals $0.00040\pm0.00013$, which corresponds to a  $2.6\sigma$ deviation from the flatness of the model, and implies a non-zero curvature of space. The implications of this finding suggest either a need for novel cosmological models or the possibility of a deviation from the standard $\Lambda$CDM model.

A key aspect of maintaining a repository over time involves updating existing files while retaining their core content. Our study focuses on maintaining files at a repository level, examining how these updated files relate to the repository's characteristics. Traditional approaches have limited success in this context, as they rely on files' full content which is significantly altered with each modification. To overcome this constraint, we developed a new file-identity identification method utilizing a multi-layer perceptron to facilitate file's long-term re-creation. By leveraging the full content and its creation timestamp, our approach enables the use of the entire content for files even after alterations. Our results show that the entire content can assist in clarifying the identities of approximately 60% of a subset of files on GitHub. Additionally, this novel meta-maintenance strategy enables access to the entire content for all files up to their creation. Through experimental validation using the entire content for all files, the effects of files' alterations on their predictability from their complete content were investigated. The experiment revealed an average files' entropy reduction following modifications, across all repositories of 19.1%, and 60.4% respectively when excluding the most frequently altered files within 1 hour of their creation. Consequently, it has been demonstrated that files' identity significantly impacts a ML model's performance in predicting files' characteristics and behaviors. The incorporation of files' entropy into repository features also led to improvements in ML models' performance metrics: +3.4% when using TF-ID

The complexity of BD And has made it difficult to determine the variations in its light and hydrogen alpha cygni line depth. Recent observations from the 6.5-m Magellan Baade Telescope and high-cadence data from TESS revealed that most of these fluctuations are caused by a single cool spot rotating with a 364.36-day period, resulting in eclipses that deviate significantly from expected patterns seen in previous studies. Notably, one eclipse is approximately 40 minutes longer than predicted. Further analysis of ECL 3, which features two cool spots rotating with a 364.36-day period, indicated that BD And displays characteristics of a Gamma Doradus variable with a notable 1mm amplitude in phase 0.5-0.6, oscillating with a period of 6.19 days.

This paper has a twofold objective. It examines the existence of solutions to the fractional Yamabe flow and investigates the implications of these solutions on the convergence of sequences of metrics on manifolds. A specific class of fractional Yamabe flows was previously proposed by Theorem 1.1 in arXiv:2010.04543. This work explores how the choice of initial conditions affects the continuity of this metric space. Notably, the fractional Yamabe flow provides a potential method for achieving scalar curvature $-1$ in the category of sDRE's.  These research components are closely related and rely on analysis of the properties of sDRE's and their interactions with manifold metrics and their associated fractional PDE's.

The primary challenge in cross-domain recommendation lies in resolving the data sparsity issue. Traditionally, this problem has been approached by leveraging shared user preferences across domains, but this often results in a loss of domain-specific information, thereby limiting its effectiveness in handling multiple sparse domains simultaneously. Moreover, user preferences are composed of various attributes, each requiring separate learning to accurately model them, which existing methods often fail to do, thereby impeding their capability to tackle multiple sparse domains simultaneously. To address these concerns, we introduce a cutting-edge solution, known as Multi-Sparse-Domain Cooperative Recommendation (MSDCR), which empowers a centralized neural network to collaborate on tackling multiple sparse data issues. Firstly, we introduce a Cross-Domain Attention (CDA) module, which aggregates user attributes and promotes cooperative learning to effectively handle the sparse data. Secondly, we propose a Cross-Domain Regularization (CDR) module, which enhances the robustness of our method by incorporating a regularizer that encourages shared user preferences. Lastly, a Complementarity Enhancement (CE) module is introduced to mitigate any potential negative influence of incongruent user attributes, thereby our model's performance is not compromised. Experimental results on five, real-world datasets, demonstrate that MSDCR consistently outperforms multiple baseline recommendation methods in terms of multiple evaluation metrics, thereby validating its superior capability in tackling multiple sparse data issues.

This research examines the deformation theory of perpendicular and symplectic bundle mappings between two manifolds. A new object, the perpendicular bundle, is introduced to analyze these mappings. It's demonstrated that the deformation theory of such mappings can be represented by an $L_{\infty}$-algebra, which builds upon the concept of the perpendicular bundle. This finding generalizes the deformation theory previously developed for isometric embeddings and harmonic maps.

Let A_{<k}(n) be the set of all partitions of n with parts of less than k unique occurrences. For instance, A_{<4}(6) consists of the following partitions: (3,2,1), (3,1^5), (2^2,1^4), (2^3,1^3), and (2^2,1^4). We find all parts of these partitions are divisible by at least 4, and set D_{\geq k}(n) as the set of all partitions of n with parts of multiples of k, and establish the equality D_{\geq 4}(n)=A_{<4}(n). We prove this equality has a dynamic programming application and show D_{\geq k}(n) < A_{<k}(n) for all n and k >= 5.

The most common statistical estimation method, least squares estimation, has been widely utilized across various fields such as economics and biology due to numerous advantages it offers. Despite its numerous benefits, researchers have not thoroughly investigated the robustness of this method in the presence of noisy data. To address the robustness issue, our study presents an enhanced variant of least squares estimation that remains effective in noisy data environments. The proposed solution is especially relevant in data reduction scenarios where the number of samples is significantly reduced. The errors resulting from this variant are bounded within a specific range of values and can be controlled to meet specific requirements. The study evaluates the method by comparing it with its standard counterpart in terms of efficiency under different levels of noise.

This study provides the production cross-sections for the $J/\psi$, $\psi(2S)$, $B_c$ and X(3872) particles in proton-proton collisions. We investigate how these cross-sections are affected by variation in scale, choice of flavour number, factorisation scheme and boundary conditions, as well as alpha-s and boundary conditions. We also examine X(3872) ratio and $B_c$ yield distributions in $p$-$p$ collisions to establish reference points for further analyses, such as those conducted at the Large Hadron Collider.

The occurrence of localization is generally associated with disorder, yet it is often associated with disorder that is non-related. In contrast, related disorder can result in related patterns of localization that persist. Utilizing numerical techniques, we investigate the effects of related disorder in the Hubbard model, a commonly studied system that contains related disorder. Our investigation focuses on the strongest form of related disorder, known as the Bond Disorder model, in which related patterns of disorder persist infinitely. Through this study, we identify distinctive characteristics of an intermediate state between ordered and disordered systems, particularly in the properties of carrier density responses at related patterns of localization, hence indicating the related nature of the disorder. Furthermore, we numerically investigate the related patterns of exponent corners utilized in related patterns of scaling analysis and discover related patterns of modifications that converge as the disorder reduces. Ultimately, our study suggests that related patterns of scaling analysis, rather than previously used numerical techniques, provide the most in-depth insight into related patterns of localization processes, enabling an investigation of related patterns of exponent corners and related parameters of the Bond Disorder model at various related patterns of lengths of the system, thus extending our understanding of related patterns of disorder in many-body systems of Hubbard type.

This study offers a theoretical basis for the reduced words in the B-type Coxeter group, building upon an extension of the fundamental theorem of combinatorics on words, and also reveals some characteristics of B-type Coxeter group related reduced words, including their length and lexicographical ordering properties.

In the absence of specific symmetry, interacting scalar field theories can still exhibit solitonic behavior, as demonstrated by two examples: the Strunz theory and an extension by the present researchers. While Strunz found a two-dimensional theory with a conserved, non-negative, and symmetry-independent scalar field, this new research adds another 2D example featuring a similar invariant, but with its value able to take negative values.

Reinforcement learning agents that learn behaviors through trial and error are generally more adaptable to various environments compared to pre-programmed algorithms. Inverse reinforcement learning, on the other hand, seeks to figure out the underlying motivation of an expert agent by observing its behavior. While invaluable in understanding why existing agents act the way they do, it often falls short of helping the developing agent perform efficiently because it doesn't provide a guarantee of better results. To address this limitation, we've developed a hierarchical inverse reinforcement learning system based on the Bayesian framework. This system not only explains the behavior of existing agents but also allows it to generalize its findings across different settings and deliver sub-optimal policies with a measurable level of confidence. At the top of this Bayesian framework is a system that models the connection between an agent's underlying motivations and its external behavior. This system is composed of multiple layers, each representing a distinct set of possible motivations for the agent's actions. As a result, we've achieved strong performance in a variety of tasks onMBLM, a new benchmark designed to evaluate why existing reinforcement learning agents act the way they do in a range of scenarios.

Building on the concept of the robust epimorphism property introduced by Drob and Kahl in 2015, specific aspects of the property have been generalised to group homomorphisms with different target groups. Specifically, an analogue has been developed for loop transfer regions, which are regions in the fundamental group of the target group that map onto the entire fundamental group of the target group through the homomorphism. It has now been decided to generalise the concept of loop transfer regions to consider subgroups of the fundamental group of the target group that map onto the entire fundamental group of the target group through the homomorphism. The generalized concept is called $\subgroup$-small loop transfer regions, which are defined as the preimages of the entire fundamental group of the target group under the homomorphism. The properties of the $\subgroup$-small loop transfer regions are then investigated in relation to normal subgroups, retraction, and free groups.

Using deep reinforcement learning in autonomous control has become increasingly effective, yet certain challenges persist. A possible solution is the integration of state estimation, but this too brings its own complications. A two-staged deep reinforcement learning approach offers a straightforward and efficient alternative. In the first stage, an state-free deep reinforcement learning model is created to design control strategies input only with reward signals. Then, these policies are translated into reward functions, enabling the development of the second agent that relies on the estimated state. This agent ultimately achieves superior performance in executing the intended control actions, and we illustrate its success in a simple stabilizing control application.

This study is the second in a series focusing on the behavior of black mass concentrations over time within the IllustrisTNG galaxy simulation project, specifically the "faithful" and "all-scale" simulations. By examining these simulations, researchers were able to track the growth and development of black holes, particularly those with high mass levels, from the early stages of the universe up to redshift 3, which marks a relatively recent period in cosmic history. According to the data obtained, virtually all black holes, even those with relatively small mass, developed within dense star clusters rather than the broader universe. As a result of interactions with surrounding matter, these black holes experienced significant growth until their masses reached approximately 10,000 times that of the sun. Although many black holes with such masses eventually merged with galaxies, those that didn't typically underwent regulated growth within a specific size range. By analyzing the distribution of these super-massive black holes at different points in time, the researchers were able to identify how their growth behavior varied with the age of the universe and density of matter. By comparing the data from the simulations to existing observational studies and theoretical models, the researchers found good overall agreement, although the simulations did show some differences from other results and were able to reproduce certain key phenomena, such as a recent upturn in the size of some active black holes and a particular pattern in the mass of super-massive black holes seen in galaxies at high density.
