Change detection is a critical task in various fields, including land use analysis and remote sensing, where detecting modifications in two images is essential. Traditionally, change detection methods compare the differences between these images and classify them as unchanged or changed. However, simply pinpointing changes isn't enough; identifying the nature of the changes is also crucial. To address this challenge, we develop an advanced approach using a Feature Combination Deep Convolutional Autoencoder (FC-DCAE) that identifies and categorizes alterations in High-Spectral Low-Spatial Resolution (HSLSR) hyperspectral images by capturing distinctive features from input images and reconstructing them effectively. The training of our model relies solely on a single reference image, allowing it to adapt to various environments without constant retraining. By evaluating our method on two hyperspectral image pairs, we observed that regions with changes were represented differently on the 2D surface compared to invariant regions, enabling us to separate them well. The outcomes demonstrate that our constructed surface provides an excellent platform for separating regions with changes from those without and classifying variations within the images.

H. B. Helfgott and A. Ruzsa introduced the concept of additive complements to the set of square numbers, proposing a problem to determine the minimum possible value of the sum of these complements within the interval from 1 to n. They established a upper limit to this sum as O(n^(7/4)), highlighting the possible improvement over the O(n^(3/2)) value achieved by Golomb. This note presents a new version with better technical details that yields the same result as them but with the potential for a reduced upper limit to this sum as O(n^(17/10)).

Quantum tunneling between valley states in silicon is studied at the atomic level, 
using silicon heterostructures that combine SiC and Si. The study shows that silicon carbide 
can act as a barrier, altering the tunneling pattern and width compared to pure silicon. 
Experiments also reveal that spin orientation within valley states significantly affects 
tunneling probability and that it can be controlled by the tip's proximity to the surface. 
The observed phenomena are in line with theoretical expectations and suggest a mechanism 
whereby tip spin is transferred to valley states without flipping, through a process 
involving the Si $p$-like states.

Nonconvex optimization problems are often overlooked in favor of more manageable convex alternatives.
However, certain nonconvex problems are essential for addressing critical real-world challenges.
In contrast, many optimization problems that are approximately convex can be resolved efficiently using well-established methods.
It is now feasible to incorporate certain nonconvex problems into this category by employing innovative strategies such as the optimality condition gradient method.
This approach readily integrates these problems into standard iterative techniques convex in nature.
We present a comprehensive, open-source software library called LibOPT that facilitates the swift development and testing of such nonconvex optimization techniques.
Features of the LibOPT framework facilitate seamless creation and execution of these techniques on both artificial and actual optimization problems.
It supports automatic generation of artificial optimization problems as well as data-driven models based on specific datasets.
Core components of the framework are built upon open-source frameworks for mathematical computations using BLAS, LAPACK, and Eigen.
Both C++ and Python interfaces are offered for maximum user accessibility.
Released under the permissive Apache 2.0 license, the framework can be accessed at https://libopt.github.io.

The concept of the transference degree of a map between homogeneous spaces was initially defined in a specific case, for configurations of type $A_1$, in a prior study. This work expands on that definition by providing a general criterion applicable to any map between uniform algebraic varieties. The new criterion confirms that the previously established condition for the transference degree on type $A_1$ homogeneous spaces is both necessary and sufficient. Additionally, this study presents specific examples, including a demonstration of a satisfactory transference degree condition yet resulting in an unsatisfactory higher transverse geometry.

In non-commutative spacetime, the relationship between spatial coordinates is defined by a constant matrix and leads to the development of non-abelian differential geometry. We employ a left contraction rule and showcase an identity crisis for right multiplication within the algebra. The non-zero contraction effect creates challenges in defining quantum particles due to the violation of the superposition principle. Furthermore, we derive modified Dirac equations and a non-standard expansion for the Dirac spinor.

We have successfully used the two-photon absorption boundary transient-current method to
trac a three-dimensional path of charge movement within a high-quality diamond crystal.
This method combines a pulsed laser and electronic circuits to map out the behavior of
semiconductors, and has been used to study synthetic diamond crystals with exceptional
transparency. By using this technique, we have not only tracked charge transport in a
diamond crystal but also mapped out the flow of charges in a two-photon absorption process.
This unique approach has enabled a detailed understanding of the dynamics of charge
traps within the diamond crystal, and has demonstrated the ability to study materials
beyond the surface level for the first time.

Our research focuses on addressing the underrepresented tasks of identifying and categorizing hate cases towards misogyny in online discourse. The standard methods for detecting hate speech have proven ineffective due to the unique nuances and link between the two tasks. To overcome this challenge, we have developed and tested deep learning models with and without a shared parameter structure, aiming to improve the overall performance on both tasks. The study also involves constructing a new dataset composed of Archaic Social Media data, highlighting the unique style characteristic of hate cases. The results of our Archaic Social Media dataset contribution and the comparison of our proposed models have significantly advanced the detection and classification of misogyny in the Arabic language.

This study solves open problems related to the existence and uniqueness of the solution for fractional backward stochastic differential equations (FBSDEs) under two key conditions: (i) the generator includes a fractional Brownian motion and is Lipschitz continuous; (ii) the generator is bounded below by a constant and Lipschitz continuous with respect to the variable b, but can be null for forward motion. When these conditions are met, we derive the solution of FBSDEs using a novel approach that involves the concept of a small $\alpha$-change and can be extended to the case where the generator is null for the variable b.

The impact of cyber attacks on control systems is a pressing concern that could have far-reaching consequences across various sectors. Current research primarily focuses on ensuring that control systems remain stable under cyber threats, but there is a pressing need for strategies that can effectively address these attacks and restore the system to its original state. This paper introduces a novel approach that enables a learning control system to remain resilient in the face of model uncertainties and adversarial actions, even when control inputs are severely restricted. This innovative framework incorporates a stochastic framework for adversarial policy search and deviates from traditional adversarial policy search by exploring an array of potentially adversarial policies instead of a singular optimal one, thereby increasing resilience and adaptability against diverse attacks. This approach is supported by the construction of a robust safe action set, ensuring that the system can remain secure and functional under diverse and unforeseen circumstances. Our experimental results showcase the efficacy of this framework in counteracting and restoring systems affected by large input and disturbance limits.

This study presents an integrated system that combines caching and distributed computation techniques, utilizing a linear network code. The overall transmission load is determined by taking the maximum of two factors: one related to caching and the other related to computation. By comparing systems that employ network code with those that don't, we've discovered that the coded system's load is consistently lower. Furthermore, we've developed an efficient method to find the optimal caching strategy in scenarios that involve a single file, where we've proven that uniformly distributing cache entries is always optimal. The concept of a 'computation cache' has been introduced to describe combined caching and computation systems, and we've applied random linear scaling analysis to obtain an approximate formula for transmission load in these situations.

We establish the Scott model of the Scott continuous semantics for the Scott continuous lambda calculus within univalent type theory. By constructing a model in univalent type theory based on Scott continuous function spaces, we prove its equivalence to the Scott model in the set-based approach. Additionally, we adapt Borel type theories to create both a Lawson and a Borel model univalent type theory, each achieving a different form of completeness. Furthermore, we develop an interpretation of positive propositions in the Scott model and prove that it satisfies the positive μ-calculus in univalent type theory, thereby resolving the decision problem for SPCF and the positive μ-calculus by reducing their validity problems to issues of univalent type theory validity.

The article presents key cancellation techniques and results of Eisenstein modules over the Jordan-Scheiner decomposition, employing finite field or $\ell$-adic variable approaches. Cancellation of poles in Eisenstein series for $GL(n,\mathbb{A}_\mathbb{Q})$ is accomplished using the Herbrand product over the Jordan-Scheiner decomposition and a application of the inclusion-exclusion principle over subsets related to generalized eigenspaces for eigenvalues along diagonal blocks in the Jordan canonical form. Furthermore, the result of Paskunas and Thorne regarding non-vanishing of Eisenstein congruences is reconstructed and proven using the proposed method.

This research explores the development of a safety-critical control system for mobile robotic arms within the context of mobile robotics and autonomous systems. The primary goal is to safeguard the arm from dangerous configurations that could lead to kinematic singularities, loss of stability, or collisions. Existing control algorithms often overlook configuration safety, which is addressed in this study through the creation of a real-time monitoring system based on a precise model of the robotic arm and its environment. The proposed solution utilizes Control Barrier Functions (CBFs) to formulate safety constraints, which are integrated into the control loop via an optimization problem, ensuring that the robotic arm remains secure at all times. The proposed method was validated using the CRoboter@IMAG and a simulation environment, which showcased the efficacy of the system in preventing the arm from entering unsafe configurations and adjusting its trajectory when necessary.

Text summarization via the extractive method employs a specific technique that identifes and selects pre-existing, non-overlapping sentences within a source text to create a concise summary. Graph-based algorithms approach this challenge by representing sentences as nodes in a graph and evaluating their relationships. In this research, various graph-based extractive summarization models are explored, incorporating different graph construction methods and attention mechanisms. Results indicate that using clustered graphs with high inter-sentence connections yields notable improvements, as demonstrated by a model combining a clustering-based graph construction method and an attention mechanism, which achieved superior performance on the SQuAD dataset.

Theorems can categorize BEC nonlinear switches into two types: those that have corresponding Ginzburg-Landau models and those that don't. This study classifies such switches shots in traps as well as in optical lattices with and without losses. Notably, some switches shots with losses can still work effectively when an appropriate compensation mechanism is applied to the loss effects.

Consider a complete K\"{a}hler manifold (M, ω) and a projective variety X, with a non-constant meromorphic map f from M to a projective space, which we denote as φ: M → P^N with a reduced indeterminacy set I(φ). Let's also define the graph of φ as Γφ and let's set the dimension of M minus the codimension of I(φ) as k. We establish a set of sufficient conditions for the distinctness of two non-constant meromorphic maps f and g from M to X when the intersection of f and g on M minus the closed set B, which is derived by taking the union of the sum of the codimensions of the relative intersections of f and g with I(f) and I(g), is considered. This is achieved when the maps satisfy specific conditions on their critical value sets and a finite set of hyperplanes with multiplicity sum N + 1 in the case of m-complete manifolds, with N + sum of the weights of the sections of the first Fuchsian type points of the maps considered to be at least 2 dim M + 1. This leads to a positive resolution for a distinctness problem, previously raised as an open question, and also provides a further understanding of a conjecture put forth by Y. Zhang.

A signature is a symmetric function taking polynomial arguments, and the signature-driven algorithm we've developed identifies the non-trivial solutions of a system of equations where each signature has a specified value. Our methodology involves establishing a an ideal specifically for non-trivial solutions and demonstrating that it's the smallest such ideal containing the given system, based on a previously established criterion. We've combined computational techniques with a strategy for explicitly constructing the ideal in question, utilizing tools like Gröbner bases and elimination methods. The approach effectively handles cases where the number of variables significantly exceeds that of the signature equations, and we demonstrate the approach through several example systems.

We present an in-depth analysis of low-energy direct photons produced in midrapidity regions of Au+Au 200 GeV and Cu+Cu 200 GeV collisions. Our study isolates thermal photons from these high-energy collisions by excluding collision-induced and hadron decay photons through subtraction methods at both central and peripheral collision points. This isolation reveals an excess of photons beyond expected outcomes in Au+Au collisions but not in Cu+Cu collisions for collision rates above 10 cross-section per b. The observation of a significant low-energy photon excess in Au+Collisions suggests that these photons originate from the quark-gluon plasma state formed during these events. Our findings also indicate a distinct difference between photon spectra of Au+Collisions and Cu+Collisions as early as five nucleon radii apart, implying an increased phase-space availability for low-energy photon production due to the higher initial density and temperature achieved in Au+Collisions compared to the threshold for QGP formation.

In 1998, Nikiforov tackled the problem of maximizing the weighted fractional chromatic number $ \chi_{\frac{d}{2}}(G) $ of a $d$-regular graph $G$ and showed that the maximum occurs for the complete $k$-partite graph $T_k^n$. He further proposed the problem of finding the second largest possible value for this weighted chromatic number, which depends on the degree $d$ and some parameters $k, r, s, t$. In 2016, Huang and Zhang proved that the maximum value for this weighted chromatic number can be expressed in terms of Levenshtein numbers, effectively resolving the long-standing problem for all values of the parameters involved.

Vector maps remove small details to reduce file size but this can negatively impact map readability. To address this issue, a novel method is proposed that efficiently removes fine details in line junctions, removing overlap and negative area information. By removing overlap and negative area information, a low computational method can be applied to reduce file size without losing essential information. Our results show that a significant reduction in processing time and storage can be achieved while maintaining high readability.

The derivation and characteristics of a new, form-preserving quasi-interpolation operator using the transcendental function exp(-γc) / (1 + vc) as its basis have been investigated. This operator maintains the property f(x) <= 0 when f belongs to C(R^n) and takes the value -infinity at the origin, and it preserves the value of functions at f(x) = 0 where f belongs to C(R^n) and has a maximum at the origin, for any positive constants v and c. Furthermore, it possesses a convergence rate of O(gamma) as gamma approaches 0, and this rate can be improved to a potentially faster rate as gamma approaches infinity at the cost of increased numerical instability. The transcendental function employed here is numerically superior in terms of conditioning and composition compared to its commonly used counterpart, which justifies the inclusion of the function v and constants sign(.) in its definition.

The detection of widespread gamma-ray shells around pulsars in the Milky Way using Fermi-LAT data, particularly at lower energies, suggests a common and previously overlooked class of objects. By analyzing Fermi-LAT's spectral characteristics and emission patterns, researchers found that these gamma-ray shells account for a significant portion of the known gamma-ray sources. To better understand their nature, our team conducted a comprehensive study on their morphology and emission properties, utilizing Monte Carlo simulations to recreate the interaction between pulsar winds and surrounding supernova remnants. The simulations, combined with X-ray data at low redshift, provided valuable insights into these objects' nature. The results support the hypothesis of a more abundant population of pulsar shells than previously thought.

Classifying images into distinct weather conditions, such as rain, snow, or other forms of precipitation, is crucial for various applications including, but not limited to, autonomous vehicle systems. Existing deep neural network architectures have achieved considerable success in this area, yet there is a notable absence of an extensive, annotated image collection specifically designed for weather detection. To address this limitation, we have compiled the first extensive dataset focused on weather recognition, featuring a custom data augmentation technique that enhances performance without compromising accuracy. Our approach involves testing multiple convolutional neural network models, ultimately demonstrating CalendarNet's superiority across multiple evaluation metrics. This study demonstrates CalendarNet's consistency in evaluating both existing and newly created architectures, highlighting the importance of choosing the right image preprocessing method and network structure to achieve optimal results.

To gauge climate change's impact on societal norms, a comprehensive model integrates scientific understanding of environmental standards with the dynamics of institutional and individual interactions. The evolution of environmental standards is influenced by three independent yet interconnected processes: scientific findings, institutional policies, and social standards rooted in human group dynamics. These processes, however, often operate independently and can be at odds with one another. To address gaps in existing research, a new study applies the cloud in-the-loop game theory to explain how social standards about climate change emerge and persists. A notable finding of this work is the existence of a new climate standard, characterized by a high threshold for acceptable climate impact, aligning with the Inter-Society Standard.

This study introduces a data-driven approach for modeling and controlling soft multi-fingered grippers derived from the properties of Koopman operator theory. The inherent linearity and non-linearity of these grippers' dynamics and constraints complicate traditional control methods. By framing the problem within the framework of data-driven linear system analysis, we achieve a simplified and controllable linear model that accurately reflects the gripper's behavior. This new approach enables the deployment of existing control strategies and ensures compliance with desired performance criteria. Furthermore, a novel control technique is proposed to facilitate precise end-effector movement at a constant speed while maintaining balanced internal forces at the fingers. Experimental validation verifies the efficacy and accuracy of our data-driven model and proposed control method.

Our research builds upon the Organic Evolutionary Algorithm by integrating the gradient descent principle into its Algebras of Operations to derive novel mutation heuristics. The primary objective of this study is to explain how gradient descent applies to EVT and illustrate its incorporation into the OEVA with source code examples.

High-redshift young radio galaxies are of great interest in the study of radio jet formation, but few examples are available for analysis at redshifts above 3. Using the Very Large Array to re-observe a previously identified field, we discovered a highly luminous radio galaxy, J2102+6015, located further away. This object, characterized by a powerful jet, reached a significantly higher optical depth in X-ray wavelengths, indicating a substantial increase in redshift to a level of 4.575. Notably, J2102+6015 is comparable in age to other established cases of high-redshift young radio galaxies. Further observations using HST revealed a complex structure in the vicinity of the core, with possible low-redshift sources and additional high-redshift objects as well as apparent absorption features. This study provides a comprehensive analysis of J2102+6015 and its unique features at high redshifts.

Prognosis of various types of lung cancer is highly complex and is often associated with errors, which is a major concern. To address these issues, we developed an accurate and robust identification system for predicting the survival rate and classification of non-small cell lung cancer using both image and patient data. Our study involved the utilization of a comprehensive, publicly accessible dataset with complete and matching image and patient information for each patient. The outcome of our model's evaluation with an independent dataset was exceptional, achieving a high level of accuracy with both the Concordance Index (CI) and Area Under the Receiver Operating Characteristic (AUROC) metrics. The predicted outcomes from our model aligned perfectly with the actual outcomes, demonstrating its high reliability and precision. Consequently, our model has the potential to significantly improve patient care by providing more accurate and reliable survival rate and classification predictions for non-small cell lung cancer.

This overview seeks to condense the essential ideas of descriptive language state representations in Markov decision processes that have been utilized in linguistic reinforcement learning research. It aims to provide the most comprehensive and concise summary possible, as many prior studies only offered brief explanations of their language state descriptions, often using very short descriptions that lacked depth. Although not an in-depth analysis of reinforcement learning, this overview seeks to describe the diverse approaches taken in the field, outlining both their strengths and limitations.

The incremental advancement of computer technology and data science enables astronomers to collect more data, but also more accurately report it. This study presents an innovative approach, combining machine learning with gravitational lensing data, to recover energy spectrum distributions without relying on predetermined assumptions about their formation. By employing k-nearest neighbor and kernelized support vector regression algorithms on 314 quasar spectra from the SDSS-DR7 catalog, along with simulated datasets, the method's efficacy is demonstrated in reconstructing the cosmic energy spectrum. Notably, with just 314 quasars, the calculated energy spectrum contrasts with the Planck's adiabatic energy spectrum within statistical margins, and predicts a cosmic energy density of $4.09^{+0.92}_{-0.72}\times10^{14} GeV m^{-3}$ at energy levels between $10^{14} GeV$ and $10^{15} GeV$ with improved accuracy compared to previous studies.

This paper thoroughly examines two types of Lie algebras, specifically the generalized finite W-algebras and the Lie algebra of derivative operators. We have developed essential characteristics of their respective irreducible highest weight representations. Additionally, we have established a key connection between the Lie algebras of derivative operators and the Lie superalgebras.

The vast amount of user-generated content on social media platforms reflects people's emotions toward various subjects, making it essential to accurately analyze their sentiments. Traditionally, this has been a challenging task, but advancements in Natural Language Processing and the ability to handle large data sets on specialized computers, known as Graph Processing Units, have enabled new approaches. One common method involves using sentiment evaluation models that RPN optimizes by incorporating regularisation techniques and optimizing the L2 norm using the Sutherland-SCHRODINGER algorithm. This improved model can then be fine-tuned using techniques such as fine-grained attention and context-based representations based on pre-trained word embeddings, ultimately leading to more accurate sentiment analysis on Twitter data.

Conversations that go beyond surface small talk often require understanding and portraying specific characteristics or roles to feel authentic. Although previous efforts to incorporate this in conversations through examples have shown some success, they struggle with sustaining the entire interaction. A new framework has been developed to maintain a consistent role throughout the conversation by providing a clear description of the desired characteristics, enabling the system to create responses that align with the intended role based on user input and system constraints. Using open-source language models without a specific knowledge base and incorporating feedback mechanisms allows the system to create responses that match expectations, which can then be fine-tuned for better performance. Extensive testing on various role definitions and user inputs demonstrates the system's effectiveness in creating natural responses that align with different role definitions and showcases promising results for future development to incorporate more nuanced features and examples.

The gravitational wave memory effect, a non-linear phenomenon, has a broader reach and is more pervasive than the conventional quadratic dependence on source mass. It exhibits higher amplitude and lasts longer at lower frequencies. It has been found that even sources as massless as binary neutron stars produce measurable signals detectable by LIGO. As the number of these sources increases, their contributions combine to form a background of gravitational waves that differ significantly from the standard gravitational wave background. This new type of background is highly frequency-dependent and exhibits a more pronounced low-frequency response and is more pervasive at nanohertz frequencies. It behaves similarly to the pulsar background discovered in the Sagnell spectrum analysis but operates at lower frequencies. This phenomenon may provide a complementary insight into cosmology and the early universe.

The loss of a specific symmetry within the MSSM under a highly energetic phenomenon, and its restoration, could trigger baryonic creation through the difference in how two distinct interactions are affected by this symmetry loss. We're investigating whether this symmetry loss could also initiate other significant cosmic events, like the generation of detectable gravitational waves through intense collisions between particles and the formation of massive black holes. We're analyzing the conditions under which these events happen using a model based on a massive field with extremely high energy, taking into account how its distribution changes over time due to quantum effects. This model suggests that this field's fluctuations could lead to significant particle collisions, the eventual merging of these collisions, and the resulting sound waves in the early universe could be detectable. Furthermore, these collisions could ultimately result in massive black holes. We're estimating the probability of this scenario's occurrence based on our understanding of the early universe's properties.

A revolutionary communication system known as semantic communication promises to comprehend and transmit the source message itself rather than its binary representation. A critical challenge in this approach involves identifying and conveying meaningful information. Our study addresses this issue by developing an artificial signaling game that incorporates causal relationships similar to those found in human signaling systems. A novel neural network model called the neuro-symbolic deep structural causal model (NS-DCSM) has been created to play this game effectively. This NS-DCSM model outperforms existing neural models in improving the system's non-linear causal structure, particularly in scenarios involving significant data loss. Our work represents a significant step towards realizing the full potential of semantic communication by integrating causal relationships into the transmission process.

In domains such as social media and online discussions, vocabulary constantly evolves, necessitating Vocabularies that adapt to emerging terms breaking existing bounds. Traditional methods of learning new words from labels are inefficient, often missing out on labeling new terms entirely. A modified approach using Naive Bayes classifies terms based on the assumption that they share the same attributes as the items they're assigned to, resulting in terms having similar distributions. Building on this, a framework is proposed that utilizes knowledge from term tag co-occurrences to refine this class membership and enhance the term prediction accuracy. This new system, NLTP, surpasses standard baselines in accuracy when testing with Twitter book titles.

Session-based recommendation systems have seen significant advancements in recent years, yet session lengths typically span only a few interactions, limiting their capacity to provide meaningful insights into user preferences. While end-of-session suggestions have been explored, they often disregard user satisfaction as session extensions can be time-consuming and inconvenient. Moreover, recommendation systems need to adapt to evolving user interests within a single session, but current models fall short in this aspect. These challenges motivate the proposal of SessionBERT with RankPreserving Representation, whose innovations include maintaining the order of user history for accurate modeling and enabling multi-task learning to tackle the difficulty of off-session interactions. Experiments demonstrate the model's superior performance and its ability to efficiently tackle off-session and dynamic re-ranking challenges in session-based recommendation tasks.

We examine the behavior of a colloidal particle that has both physical and chemical properties, specifically its translations and rotations, within two-dimensional environments. To model the particle's movement, we use the Segr\'e-Schmieden potential, which takes into account the forces of friction and activity and generalizes the well-known Kim-Szekrenys point activity. By applying the Fokker-Planck equation, we demonstrate that the particle exhibits a dynamic equilibrium distribution that is independent of its initial state. Furthermore, we explore the effects of activity on the particle's distribution and mobility in various environments and demonstrate that, even with symmetry, a particle can exhibit properties of direction, specifically, it may preferentially move forward or backward at a distance from the source of activity.

Our proposed method utilizes the Finite Variation principle to formulate three-dimensional simulation equations for the Geological Fracture Network, which we then solve using the Mixed-Finite Variation method. By leveraging an unstructured conforming mesh composed of hexahedral cells, we ensure stability and accuracy in our models. Furthermore, we successfully implemented our method in our 3D simulation software incorporating both matrices and fractures.

The maintenance of geometric formations by flying vehicles such as vehicles and aircraft relies on advanced navigation systems that utilize Global Navigation Satellite Systems (GNSS). However, GNSS is prone to errors or disruptions caused by obstacles or deliberate interference. Consequently, relying solely on GNSS increases the risk of collisions. To mitigate this issue, our solution involves utilizing proximity sensors as a fallback when GNSS is compromised, but this would result in the loss of the geometric shape of the fleet. To rectify this, we have developed a novel method that incorporates the Belhumeur-Simard-Davidson algorithm to align the fleet based on sensory data, thus preserving the geometric shape and preventing collisions even when switching between GNSS and proximity sensors.

In graph theory, the Seidel matrix of a graph G is defined based on its adjacency matrix, where its entries represent the complement of graph G's relationships. The Seidel spectrum of G refers to the eigenvalues of this matrix. This paper focuses on determining the maximum possible range and Seidel energy of a graph G with n vertices and a specific graph type known as the chain graph, denoted as C_{n-1}.

Our study investigates a novel mean-field optimal control problem using a stochastic differential equation with fractional Brownian motion. The optimal control problem involves finding the best control to minimize the expected cost of a system over time. The resulting value function, which represents the minimum expected cost starting with a given state, is proven to satisfy a specific partial differential equation with a terminal condition. This proof is based on verifying that a certain viscosity solution to the partial differential equation is smooth enough.

The properties of a Dirac operator with non-real spectra are examined, where the spectra are a union of two elliptic finite bands of real values. The research focuses on a scenario with constant magnetization, and spectra that are symmetric around zero. The analysis reveals a zero-index for the operator's associated elliptic self-adjointization under these conditions. Additionally, under a quasi-periodic scenario, the operator's zero-index persists provided the quasi-period is an element of a specific, countable subset of real numbers. However, if the quasi-period is not an element of this subset, the operator exhibits a non-trivial, real-valued, and non-zero topological invariant, known as the Chern number. This invariant can take the values of $\pm 2$. The inherent Dirac magnetic ellipses show a Z_2 symmetry for all magnetization types and demonstrate a duality relationship based on the elliptic T-dual of their generalized K-dual. Furthermore, the ellipses' shapes and types demonstrate a correspondence to local and global topological invariants of the Dirac operator's spectra.

The recent emergence of V2X has its roots in various applications that facilitate safer driving and improved road operations, such as collision avoidance and optimized traffic lights. In scenarios where the density of Roadside Units is low, the potential of V2X can go unrealized and traffic safety features may be compromised. To overcome this limitation, the implementation of relays has been introduced to bridge communication gaps. Our work specifically explores network diverse diversity in 2-tier vehicle-to-vehicle communication networks incorporating both diverse channel statistics and relays. Notably, we consider a scenario where the diversity order exceeds two by positioning the relay at a suitable distance. We derive closed-form expressions for key performance indicators including outages, diversity, and two-layer combined diversity. We also investigate the impact of key parameters on performance and demonstrate through theoretical analysis that higher mobility of roadside units favors relays, whereas optimal behavior is observed in terms of relay and vehicle positions.

Currently, approximately 24% of articles on English Wikipedia are categorized
as requiring enhancement or improvement, yet manually adding this classification
to every new article is impracticable. We've developed an automated system that
analyzes new article edits in real-time, detecting patterns associated with
low-quality materials and  adding the appropriate low-quality tags accordingly.
The automated process can also be utilized to re-evaluate existing uncategorized
articles to identify those that should be improved. Our system was implemented
on 24,211 articles, of which 7% were reclassified as potentially low-quality,
and the manual review of our algorithm's recategorized articles confirmed its
validity. Notably, our model correctly predicted 96% of newly created article edits
that were subsequently labeled as low-quality by human editors.

Deep neural networks have achieved remarkable success in the field of image classification, but their black-box nature and training requirements raise concerns about energy efficiency and transparency. Adversarial examples have exposed the security flaws in their training processes. However, their creation typically involves extensive manual input and does not address these issues fully. This research presents a novel method for generating adversarial examples through a framework where the models are only observed output without access to internal structures, effectively treating them as complete mysteries. By using generative models, the authors can train white-box adversaries with far less effort than traditional black-box methods and apply them to multiple target models with significant success rates, outperforming the black-box approach by large margins while requiring minimal adjustments.

Researchers have observed the decay $b\to s$ into a $D^0$ meson and a $K_L$ kaon, specifically in the $B^0_s$ meson's decay to these particles. Their findings align with expectations. Furthermore, they have gathered substantial evidence supporting the $B^0_s$ meson decaying into a $D^0$ and $\bar{K}$ or $D^0$ and $K^+$ meson. These outcomes stem from a dataset comprising $p\bar{p}$ collisions at 13 TeV, with a luminosity of 5 inverse femtobarns, and analyses conducted via the LHCb detector as of June 2018.

We examine geometric geometric T-duality within the framework of twisted tori.
It's observed that geometric T-duality constructs an inverse to the simplified T-duality 
formulated in twisted K-theory. Moreover, specific forms of geometric T-duality correspond to 
various forms of graph T-duality.

Reinforcement learning shows great promise in guiding humans through complex tasks. However, the high level of expertise needed to design effective reward functions limits its practical applications. By leveraging co-observation of human interactions, the approach of transfer learning enables skills to be transferred across different people; nevertheless, it relies on observing unsuccessful attempts, which is often impractical. In a novel variation of transfer learning, our method utilizes co-observation without requiring the observation of failure, making it suitable for demonstrating and transferring complex skills to other humans. We identify and formalize the problem's unique challenges and compare two potential solutions: a supervisor-assisted approach and an autonomous method. Through extensive simulations, we validate that our proposed autonomous method outperforms the supervisor-assisted approach, and we use this results to further enhance its efficiency while minimizing the demands on the agent's capabilities.

This paper analyzes two key aspects of Probabilistic Arithmetic Compression: the PAC distance and the probabilistic compression ratio. The PAC distance quantifies the dissimilarity of two data sources by evaluating the expected length difference of compressed data under one source when data is drawn from the other source. The probabilistic compression ratio represents the maximum PAC distance between a source and all possible data sources. We conduct a thorough investigation of these concepts, comparing them to established information-theoretic metrics like the Kullback-Leibler divergence and relative entropy, and examine the impact of code optimization on these metrics.

The intersection of computer vision and neuroscience holds great potential to transform how we approach visual tracking and reconstruction of complex movements. To tackle this, our research focuses on creating an efficient system for concurrently monitoring the hands' movements and understanding their interactions with objects in uncontrolled environments. Our proposed method involves converting complex video footage into a more manageable point cloud format while preserving essential spatial and temporal characteristics. Next, we transform this point cloud into a series of learned representations, enabling accurate tracking of hand movements and the creation of detailed 3D models of objects. Finally, by integrating this tracking data into a point cloud sequence, we can reconstruct the original video's content while maintaining high fidelity to the original scenes. Our approach demonstrates remarkable results, showing significant improvements over existing state-of-the-art techniques, with a PCK@10 of 27.6% for hand tracking and better than random performance for hand pose estimation in video sequences.

This study examines C-groups with a grade of 4 and an interlacing number of 2 that don't correspond to crystallographic systems. A comprehensive list of such groups is provided along with their associated non-crystallographic Coxeter graphs.

Developing robots that can understand and navigate in 3D environments is a difficult problem due to the need for extensive calibration of depth-sensing robots and the cost associated with this process. Our solution involves training a robot to learn depth-sensing calibration on its own, along with learning to estimate the exact position of its end-effector. A key aspect of our approach is the use of a new self-supervised loss function, called the auto-calibration or AC loss, to verify and refine the robot's estimated 3D world view. Experimental results show that our method outperforms existing solutions by a large margin and is capable of calibrating the robot's depth-sensing capabilities more efficiently.

Under a specific interference framework attributed to K-nearest-neighbors, interference only occurs between units based on their spatial proximity. Building upon this concept, the study develops two alternative approaches to detect treatment interference beyond neighboring units. Firstly, an augmented regression framework is created, comprising two stages, with the second stage regression coefficient serving as an indication of beyond-neighboring unit interference. The coefficient's significance can also inform the optimal neighborhood size. Secondly, a model selection criteria, specifically AIC, is adapted for the purpose and applied to choose the most suitable neighborhood size. Both theoretical and empirical evidence demonstrate the effectiveness of these developments.

Investigating the properties of Neutron Stars serves as an effective means to explore Beyond the Standard Model physics. As a compact and dense environment, it's optimal for annihilation processes of Dark Matter, leading to substantial energy emission. This energy can alter the formation process of Neutron Stars by modifying its equation of state through quantum effects. Thus, understanding the specifics of this energy is essential to enhancing our knowledge about Dark Matter and its impact on astrophysical bodies. To this end, we have refined the calculation of neutrino emissivity in Dark Matter annihilation, considering pseudoscalar-mediated interactions, thereby refining our earlier studies that focused on the vector coupling. Our updated approach considers three scenarios: direct neutrino emission from Dark Matter annihilation into neutrinos; Zhigadlo process involving virtual Zenon particles; and direct emission during the Zenon decay of a state composed of two electrons and two positrons. To validate our findings, we have applied our results to the pulsar neutron star RX J1933+2117, deriving the pseudoscalar coupling constant of Dark Matter to electrons and its annihilation cross-section. Our analysis reveals that our estimated values of the coupling and annihilation cross-section fall within experimentally defined constraints.

I've introduced ShapePipe, a sophisticated pipeline that measures the shapes of celestial objects, particularly very distant galaxies, by accounting for perspective effects. Since these effects can be difficult to interpret for such galaxies, I've created an工作流程 that automatically updates a lensing model by analyzing the relationship between galaxy distance and measurement, thereby minimizing accuracy issues associated with traditional models. Using this approach, I applied shape measurements to Unanggui/Canada-France-Ile-de-France Survey data of extremely distant galaxies, achieving an accuracy of 1.1 percent at a redshift of 3, and demonstrating that our model outperforms conventional models, particularly when analyzing high-redshift galaxies. ShapePipe is an open-source solution, accessible at the provided URL, and is designed to be adaptable for other galaxy survey projects requiring advanced galaxy measurement analysis.

Consider an $m \times n$ matrix $D$ composed of rational entries, divided into four submatrices based on whether its rows or columns are zero. We extend the classical Kronecker-Weyl theorem by adapting it to these specific rational structures. Additionally, we apply a similar concept to diagonal matrices in $\mathbb{R}^m$, and explore connections with the Hall approximation, establishing links between these general equidistribution outcomes and diophantine approximation.

We prove that for any complete intersection singularity, the properties of being
Du Bois over a field of positive characteristic and rational over a closed prime
characteristic are equivalent. This equivalence resolves the Du Bois version of
Illusie's conjecture and the Rational version of Illusie's conjecture for this
specific case.

It has been experimentally demonstrated in a field-adjustable hexagonal spin-1/2 Heisenberg model that Berezinskii-Kosterlitz-Thouless correlations can be achieved within a single point of the magnetic phase diagram. A study of the system's response in the chi' susceptibility and spin spiral correlations reveals that these are enhanced within a specific region of the phase diagram that borders a ferromagnetic state. Notably, these correlations exhibit a correlation length of approximately 10 unit cells, the highest observed in a Heisenberg model with an anisotropy less than the exchange interaction. The development of an effective spin model based on classical Monte Carlo simulations allows for a in-depth understanding of correlation dynamics, resulting in a detailed mapping between the classical model and the Kagome Heisenberg model.

Modifying the standard model to include $N_1$ and $a$ for a sterile neutrino and an axion respectively,  is a logical response to the strong CP problem and neutrino oscillation problems. This results in complex interactions between them with additional effects on cosmological phenomena. This interaction leads to unique phenomena such as the Axion-Sternile Neutrino Shadow Substance, which has potential to resolve multiple issues in cosmology, such as dark matter, neutrino mass, and neutrino non-gaussianity problems. This research explores the viability of the proposed model through theoretical, astrophysical, and cosmological analyses and predicts testable outcomes for future neutrino oscillation, CMB, BBN, gravitational wave, and neutrino non-gaussianity studies.

Upcoming quantum computers will have the ability to solve complex problems, although they require access to specialized quantum states known as magic states. The key measurement, magic state distillation, is limited by the amount of classical data needed to generate these states. Our research provides a measure to determine the minimum amount of data required and, in turn, limits the maximum classical data a distillation process can access. This discovery enhances previous research and offers new insights into the connection between quantum state generation and classical resources.

Our research explores a dynamic dark energy model based on the Tsallis entropy principle in various cosmological models. We investigate the behavior of this energy by analyzing acceleration and deceleration phases through state equations and weak dominance conditions. We propose a parameterized model in the form of a complex quintessence field, written as $\Phi = \Phi_1 + \Phi_2$, where $\Phi_1$ influences the decelerating phase and $\Phi_2$ affects the accelerating phase. We derive equations for the energy density and dark pressure as functions of the complex quintessence field, specifically $\rho(\Phi)$ and $P(\Phi)$. Taking into account the properties of the Tsallis entropy, we calculate the holographic dark energy density as $\rho_D = \frac{1}{L_N^2}$, where $L_N$ is the relevant length scale linked to Tsallis entropy. We demonstrate that the energy dynamics can be controlled by a Hubble radius $L_\Lambda = \frac{1}{H}\left(1-\frac{\Phi_1^\beta}{\Phi_c^\beta} \right)$, highlighting the impact of $\Phi_2$ on accelerating the universe.

Ground-based wide-field surveys like the Large Multi-Object Image Spectrograph (LAMOST) are instrumental in collecting astronomical spectra efficiently, making it suitable for various projects such as transient searches across diverse categories like supernovae, asteroids, outbursts, novae, and recurrent novae. Recently, LAMOST conducted four $K$2 plates over three nights in 2020 to collect spectra of the entire sky in the visible range for a total of 160,154 sources on each night. These entire sky surveys provide valuable insights into various phenomena such as transient cosmic events, outbursts, and outbursts of different types of stars, contributing to our understanding of the universe's dynamics and evolution. Our study presents the initial findings from four $K$2 plates, focusing on transient searches, and reveals the diversity of detected objects, including supernovae, outbursts, and other phenomena, as well as their distribution patterns. The exploration also reveals the existence of a peculiar nova classified as a possible jet-driven nova and several objects worthy of in-depth study, contributing to our understanding of the cosmos and its evolution. Our findings suggest the potential of LAMOST in detecting a variety of transient objects, and the collected data is available for further research online.

Recent breakthroughs in SRAM design have made it possible to utilize SRAM caches as compact, cost-effective sources of true random numbers. The SRAM's stochastic electron behavior, specifically trap-assisted tunneling, can be leveraged to generate genuine random numbers. Previous methods of detecting SAT has involved time-based measurements using timer circuits, though visibility of IR drop was limited due to timing constraints. Our research presents a novel methodology for measuring IR drop across an SRAM supply line by analyzing buffer output voltages without relying on additional timer circuits. By detecting fluctuations in the SRAM supply voltage, we were able to generate high-entropy random data at a significantly enhanced data rate of 5 Mbits/sec. The rate of random number generation through our method surpassed existing techniques by a factor of 5-10, while material and layout costs were increased by a mere 1%. The integration of a 64-bit seed and the application of a hash function enable the production of a continuous data stream at 5 Mbits/sec without depletion. Our results indicate a 95 \% confidence interval in the statistical distribution of the generated random numbers through a test based on NIST statistics.

A novel molecular resistive memory based on single-electron tunneling has been developed, utilizing a redox molecule that's sandwiched between electron source and drain molecular quantum dots. The research focuses on a ferrocene molecule coupled with molecular dots made of benzene-diterithium and pyridine-coplatinum, respectively, while simulating the electrical characteristics with a quantum transport method called non-equilibrium Green's function, to understand the underlying redox-driven mechanism. We show that the conduction pathway is spin-polarized, which may provide the foundation for spin-polarized current detection in redox chemistry. Furthermore, the study reveals dot-anion instability in one configuration, which could lead to stochastic effects. We outline the design of single-electron resistive switches based on molecular electron transport and identify dot design considerations to mitigate stochastic effects. We also highlight the role of molecular dot charge- and symmetry-based design in tuning the on/off current. We propose a two-terminal single-electron resistive switch, composed of molecular components with stable cation and anion forms, which could operate over a wide temperature range without external light. We've devised an equivalent circuit to study the stochastic effects and suggest a multi-dot configuration to mitigate stochastic effects by utilizing stochastic fluctuations to switch between high and low resistance states, enabling the creation of single-electron resistive switches for analog and digital molecular memory applications.

The scale-setting features of loop integrals are examined using the technique of topological causal depiction. An explicit algorithm is provided for determining the algebraic expressions of multi-loop on-shell integral scale-setting graphs. The method employed utilizes the overall loop numbers and propagator counts of subgraphs within a given graph. It is demonstrated that the overall graph degree can be expressed as the sum of the products of each graph's loop number and the count of its corresponding subgraphs. Furthermore, numerical evaluations of numerical integral functions reveal that the most significant contributions to these functions come from graphs with sequential loop stacking. This has been confirmed by carrying out numerical assessments in four dimensions.

We have developed a comprehensive eigenstate expansion formula for one-dimensional two-level quantum walkers using the Jansen and van der Pol model, which we applied to analyze how initial coin operations and evolution time impact the walker's localization behavior and ultimately its final distribution.

The stars under consideration consist of conventional hadrons enveloping a quark core, whose boundary is defined by the transition from an MIT-bag-like to a mixed bag-quark phase, identified through specific conditions met in the radial distribution of hadron and quark pressures. To fulfill these conditions, the presence of Omega baryons, denoted by their symbol $\Omega$, is crucial. Employing the NJL model, we determined the radial profiles of specific baryon and meson properties, leading to predictions of considerable enhancements in their core concentrations. As a result, we predicted a significant rise in the maximum mass of such composite stars, allowing for fully quarked stars to remain compatible with existing observations. Additionally, we found that composite stars, whether with a core composed of neutrons, a proton, or an $\Omega$-baryon, can be distinguished from one another through a specific characteristic, represented by the ratio between the mass radius and the radius of the core. A higher ratio corresponds to a $y$-shaped profile, whereas the presence of an $\Omega$-baryon leads to a concave profile, characterized by a gradually decreasing quark-core in the stellar interior.

The research investigates the q-deformation effects on optical slow-fast light phenomena in a specific optomechanical setup containing a q-deformed laser, material, and mechanical resonator. It is discovered that optically inducing slow and fast light within this system is feasible. Experimental results show that the optical susceptibility and refractive index in the q-deformed optomechanical system exhibit complex behaviors influenced by the deformation parameter q. Notably, the transmission coefficient and q-deformation exhibit an inverse relationship. Conversely, the imaginary transmission coefficient shows a converse interaction, exhibiting a periodic and non-linear response to variations in the deformation parameter q.

Adverse-admission scissors modes, involving a mixture of admission and inverse admission, are key to a deeper understanding of nuclear interactions. The absence of specific isospin conditions allows for their occurrence, while their presence is marked by specific magnetic dipole transitions between adjacent isotopes. A theoretical understanding of these scissors modes, however, remains limited. This work provides a theoretical framework for adverse scissors modes, using a model based on two rotating components, where one represents proton-dominant dripline nuclei and the other represents neutron-dominant ones. Neutron and proton滴线核, used as boundaries for this model, have distinct features on it. Using this model, researchers were able to successfully predict certain measurable properties, including excitation energies and magnetic dipole transition probabilities for specific nuclei, including $^{146}$Sm, where they matched experimental results accurately.

Understanding the dynamics of ultrathin oxide films grown on substrates via epitaxy is crucial for observing complex behaviors. Such a model system involves extremely thin films, where multiple factors influence their dynamics: substrates, epitaxy, and molecular bonding. Due to epittaxy, initial film growth follows a curved trajectory, leading to rotation, distortion, and eventual flattening into a smooth surface over extended periods. Our research utilizes high-speed imaging and advanced image processing techniques to analyze film dynamics in real-time, elucidating the dynamics of these models systems and facilitating exploration of similar systems' behavior.

We explore the behavior of atoms cooled by an array of optical cavities from a combined quantum perspective that considers the atoms and the cavity systems as intertwined quantum entities. By analyzing fluctuations in the cavity intensity and the atoms' distribution, correlations are revealed, particularly in situations involving strong atom-cavity interactions. Merely looking at the atoms and ignoring the cavities is sufficient to detect these correlations, as demonstrated by the observation of non-Gaussian distributions, skewness, and the breakdown of the Poisson model's effectiveness.

A dataset consisting of 600 prominent cryptocurrencies over a period of a year has been analyzed using methods like network modeling and time series analysis. The analysis considered both individual, two-way and higher order influences, incorporating transaction volumes into account. Contrary to expectations, both individual, collective and higher order influences showed increased volatility on weekends compared to weekdays, likely due to reduced market activity. Furthermore, exchanges have significant collective impact on the market more so than individual coins. When it comes to individual coins, cryptocurrencies with higher market capitalization show the weakest day-off influence, whereas coins near the top 10% show the weakest collective and higher order influences.

Recent theoretical and experimental investigations into the formation of new particles in gas-phase reactions between sulfuric acid and water have highlighted the significance of nucleation processes in the growth of aerosols cloud formation. A key factor affecting this process is the nucleation rate, which is heavily dependent on the cluster mass partition function. However, the impact of zero-point motion on this function and, in turn, on the nucleation rate in small molecular clusters, particularly at the interface between classical and quantum mechanics, remains unclear. To better understand this effect, we have employed high-precision ab initio calculations to analyze the mass partition functions of small cluster systems of up to 12 molecules, taking into account the vibrational zero-point motion's influence. Our results, which demonstrate the importance of accurate frequency calculations, show that the impact of zero-point motion can significantly vary and should not be overlooked in accurate mass partition function predictions and future mass spectrum studies.

This study introduces the concept of compact recognition compacta that generalize recognized compacta. It also defines and investigates the compact space of equivariant non-expansive function recognition, which集合 contains all such functions from a compact metric domain to the non-negative real numbers. The research demonstrates that this function space possesses the property of being a CMR-compacta of a specific type and that it also possesses a unique, positively charged zero-dimensionality characteristic.

In one spatial dimension, an analog of the gravitational effect of velocity drag can be found in the thermal Hall response. By applying linear response theory and considering asymmetric interactions, we show that this analogy is not comparable as it relies on further assumptions. The analog of velocity drag does not provide insight into viscoelastic properties or transport coefficients. The Einstein relation connects mobility and susceptibility, whereas the thermal Hall effect's coupling between velocity and energy current is better described by a relation that connects this coupling and energy current susceptibility. This new relation is derived directly from the one-loop kinetic theory, thus deriving the Kohn-Luttinger relation. The relation also has broader applicability beyond kinetic theory, including hydrodynamic models.

The primary objective of regularizing a model is to control its overfitting by imposing a constraint on its performance, with the model's complexity being the primary factor considered in most studies. This project challenges that assumption by exploring geometric complexity as a critical element in shaping the model's structure and its impact on overfitting. By examining the geometric properties of neural networks through the lens of topology, calculus, and algebra, this research reveals the existence of straightforward neural networks characterized by repetitive patterns and straightforward shapes. The analysis shows that simple neural networks are more efficient in terms of storing information and are more likely to generalize well on unseen data. As a result, the study proposes the development of novel regularization techniques centered on geometric complexity to enhance prediction accuracy.

Assessing the Wilson coefficients for $B^0\to K^{*0}\mu^+\mu^-$ decays necessitates a thorough examination of multiple resonant and non-resonant processes, allowing for an immediate analysis of the muon-based Wilson coefficient $C_{10}$ without further statistical reductions. This evaluation relies on the LHCb dataset comprising 189 pb$^{-1}$ of $pp$ collisions at $\sqrt{s}=7$ TeV. The coefficient $C_{10}$ is determined through a combination of likelihood fits applied to a large dataset and background subtraction methods applied to additional data. A comprehensive understanding of the phase space of $B^0\to K^{*0}\mu^+\mu^-$ decays is also required, which involves accounting for the impact of hadronic form factors. This study focuses on the most accessible QCDC modes where form factor effects are minimized. With a total $C_{10}$ normalization obtained from $B^0\to K^+\mu^-\nu$ decays via the muon-based channel, this coefficient is found to be $-0.037\pm 0.013$ and exhibits a slight negative deviation of $1.9\sigma$ from the Standard Model. The quality of school children's written essays has become a vital indicator of educational quality, prompting schools to seek reliable assessment methods. As an alternative to traditional evaluation, automated essay evaluation (AEE) has been explored for over two decades, with varying levels of success. In contrast to past AEE approaches, which treated papers as sequences of words, recent studies have treated them as sequences of sentences. Our study delves into the efficacy of AEE using the latest transformer models and the impacts of several modifications on the original BERT model. We also investigate how adding supplementary data using two different methods affects AEE performance, utilizing an existing AEE dataset and several datasets compiled for the study. Our findings indicate that using a pre-trained BERT model as a feature extractor for feature enrichment significantly improves AEE results, with scores advancing from 62.93 to 69.96 on the TUES dataset and from 54.36 to 57.38 on the Korean KoreanEssay dataset.

In the realm of multivariate statistics, there is a crucial need to analyze the relationship between the extreme values of multiple variables. Various methodologies have been proposed to address this requirement. This report aims to consolidate the most significant methods for capturing extreme dependencies and discuss the challenges associated with each approach.

This research examines how intergenerational movement changes as opportunities are taken away or created gradually. A theoretical model explores how unequal distribution of chances affects family advancement over generations, with findings revealing that small opportunities can significantly impact long-term social equity.

The symmetry of the wave function for non-relativistic particles is linked to the spin-statistics connection by providing an odd number of factors in the parity argument. These factors establish the connection between spatial location and the wave function's symmetry. To prevent the wave function from being identically zero, the parity of these spatial location factors must compensate for the connection between spin and statistics.

We introduce an upgraded RingCT protocol that supports multi-signature addresses, 
allowing users to opt for a set of signers whose signatures are required to spend 
from that address, among which one must belong to the sender, who then signs the 
transaction and forwards it to the network, acting as the leading node in the 
transaction process. This reduction in required signatures leads to reduced transaction 
sizes and costs, while maintaining complete privacy. Additionally, to minimize 
verification time for recipients, we incorporate Groth arguments instead of Bellare 
arguments, substituting 480+ bytes with just 220 bytes at the expense of adding around 
200 bytes for verification of the sender's identity, thus optimizing verification 
efficiency.

The concept of space toughness for computational problems was explored by
Mountjoy and Ryser earlier this year. Building on their foundational work, we
expand on their results specifically in relation to structured linear equations.
We demonstrate the following outcomes: (1) an improved reduction from dense
systems to sparse systems, yielding a q-space and equivalent-bq time
complexity of O(n log^2(n)/cr^2(q)) and O(nr cr^2(q) log^2(n)), respectively; (2)
a proven space-toughness result for the sparse system solved via Coppersmith-
Schwartz methods, resulting in O(n^2/c^2) as a lower bound; (3) an optimal
space-toughness result for the dense system, yielding a c^2/n^2 variance; (4)
optimal space-toughness results for the Cholesky and LU factorizations; (5)
a proven space-toughness result for finding a symmetric square root of a
positive definite matrix; (6) space-toughness results for triangular
factorizations of triangular and banded matrices; (7) space-toughness results
for Cholesky and LU factorizations of triangular matrices; (7) space-toughness
results for solving upper triangular and tridiagonal systems; (8) space-toughness
results for the matrix tree determinant and quadratic forms.

The LHCb experiment at the CP5 configuration, utilizing 123 nb$^{-1}$ of 13 TeV proton-proton collisions, was examined to examine the simultaneous production of three massive gauge bosons. Results showed that after accounting for potential backgrounds from standard model processes and a hypothetical scenario lacking flavor change, no evidence of these three-gauge-boson interactions was found. This led to establishment of 95% confidence level upper limits on the occurrence rates for various possible combinations of vector bosons. Notably, the occurrence rates for various possible combinations of vector bosons were established to be significantly below predicted values from theoretical models, including possible scenarios driven by new physics beyond the standard model.

In this study, we address the limitations of existing UD Hebrew parsing frameworks, which encompass diverse text types such as news and religious texts. Our research aims to expand the current framework by incorporating an additional corpus of 18k Mafren texts, which we utilize to fine-tune and assess the performance of the already developed UD Hebrew parsing model. Our results demonstrate that fine-tuning substantially enhances data coverage and induces only minor variations in data balance. Furthermore, we found that the model's parameters optimally adapt to the new corpus's characteristics, yielding the best parsing accuracy on both the original and new datasets. Our findings also suggest that the choice of training history and initial parameters significantly impacts the model's performance and should be carefully evaluated. Ultimately, we suggest that the optimized model and parameters serve as a solid foundation for the continued development of the UD Hebrew parsing task.

We investigate the dimension of our new $\varepsilon$-isometric concept and demonstrate its effectiveness by showing that the dimension significantly decreases for incompressible subsets of the incompressibility constant $I(X)$. We also define a specific characteristic for this metric dimension and establish relationships with other scale-invariant concepts. We further demonstrate a property related to商 mappings that results in both an increase and decrease of this dimension.

Recent efforts in science are shifting focus from simple data collection to the collaborative integration of existing knowledge within research communities, alongside empirical data acquisition and analysis. In science and engineering fields, simulations have historically been key tools for this purpose, yet existing approaches to community-wide modeling fall short due to their reliance on centralized control, limited scope to particular communities, and lack of effectiveness in harnessing the full potential of web technologies. We propose an open-source web platform for collaborative data-informed modeling, rooted in the principles of web semiotics and semanterity. We will illustrate the utility of this system through an example of collaborative groundwater flow analysis, incorporating insights from literature, expert opinions, field measurements, and relevant scientific theories.

We examine the performance of LDPC codes with varying degree distributions on the binary erasure channel (BEC). The analysis is based on comparing degree degree relationships and includes finding the optimal binary erasure channel capacity where absorption can occur for ensembles with uniform degree distributions. We also explore the implications of this optimal capacity in relation to the binary erasure channel and propose methods for LDPC code design based on the results. It is shown that these codes can be absorbed at capacities exceeding the channel's actual capacity. Absorption can be achieved with simple two-degree LDPC codes. We suggest a design method for uniform LDPC codes with two degrees that is more robust than the optimal codes. Absorption can be achieved with two degrees and only two degrees of freedom in this design method. Ultimately, this design approach yields sub-optimal LDPC codes that are sufficiently good for practical use.

A predictive filter for discrete-time linear systems with delayed control input is developed within the System Level Synthesis framework. This new constraint, arising from all possible trajectories of the closed loop system, enables the creation of novel constraints over predictive states, thus expanding the set of admissible predictive states. An optimal cost function state-dependent and quadratic in nature is created, which allows for the optimization of the predictive state variance through an efficient quadratic program. Predictive safety constraints over the predictive state can be formulated directly from the novel admissible set of predictive states thus expanding the set of admissible predictive states. This new constraint, which considers all possible trajectories, leads to the identification of the minimal set of initial conditions that能保证系统安全. An attractive characteristic of this filter is its offline computability. Furthermore, when applied to a flexible link manipulator with a delayed torque input, the proposed filter proves its robustness in handling difficult control conditions.

We developed a new attack against the standard decoy-state quantum key distribution system which relies in part on the phase randomization principle. By exploiting the typical implementation of phase randomization using electro-optic modulators (EOMs), we successfully deceived the legitimate users into believing that the security criteria were being met, while actively disrupting the key generation process and manipulating the key key. In specific scenarios, our proposed attack has the potential to not only disrupt the key generation process, but also to generate biases in the final key. Moreover, we demonstrated that even if the use of EOMs is avoided in favor of other media for generating phase randomness, a nonnegligible binary bias in the key can still be achieved by the attacker.

The performance of various K-way classification methods was compared to that of a newer, unified approach called in-context learning (ICL) by a large-language model (LLM). In our study, the ICL method was implemented using OpenAI's GPT-3.5 language model. Through comprehensive experiments across multiple domains, the results revealed that the pretraining dataset of an LLM significantly influences its ability to perform well with the ICL approach. Moreover, our analysis revealed discrepancies between expected and actual results, showing that a pretraining dataset does not always produce the anticipated improvements in model output. In contrast, the results were more in line with expectations under the zero-shot chain-of-thought (CoT) approach. In addition, our findings demonstrated the sensitivity of both the CoT and ICL methods to prompts. Finally, our research also demonstrated the impact of pretraining dataset source on the ability of LLMs to generalize effectively.

The morphology of a galaxy cluster's central area can be categorized as either smooth or fragmented. There's still debate about the factors responsible for its fragmented state, with some researchers suggesting the influence of turbulence and others pointing to radiative cooling. By employing 3D MHD simulations, we examined the relationship between these variables. Our results demonstrate that gas fragmentation can arise solely from radiative cooling without the need for turbulence, with the presence of turbulence intensifying this fragmentation. Furthermore, we investigated how factors such as gas turbulence, magnetic field alignment, and electron thermal conduction affect the cluster's properties, including the instability of fluctuations, fluctuations' expansion, magnetic field evolution, and conduction. Our simulations revealed that fragmentation tends to occur along field lines, with MHD modes like the Kelvin-Helmholtz instability playing a crucial role in the expansion of these fragments. In scenarios with high-temperature to density ratios and significant radiative losses, the fragmentation scale decreases. The comparison between various physical processes showed that radiative cooling produces the smallest fragments, with other processes like turbulent mixing introducing additional energy and reducing density further, which in turn generates even smaller fragments through radiative cooling. Conversely, turbulent mixing may blend fragments and lead to further fragmentation. Numerical tests of the Kelvin-Helmholtz instability confirmed that it drives the expansion and blending of the cluster's clouds faster than predicted by non-radiative processes alone, playing a crucial role in morphology evolution.
