To overcome this limitation and harness the potential of visually-rich document features for enhanced extraction accuracy, we incorporate rich multimodal architectures directly into the extraction model framework, leading to improved performance in complex document extraction scenarios that require cross-table relationships and feature integration. However, these rich models' potential is hampered by their elevated training costs, especially when compared to their more computationally-efficient counterparts. To overcome these limitations and reduce their reliance on precisely-aligned training data, we shift to more pragmatic data-labeling strategies by embracing labeled data with imperfect alignments and loosely-crafted annotations. To accommodate these changes, we extend traditional evaluation metrics to accommodate scenarios in which full feature aggregation is not feasible due to data misalignment. Ultimately, these adaptations enable the development of rich document extraction models using imperfectly-aligned data, thereby making their widespread adoption in commercial document processing more feasible and accessible.

Our study focused on the EuS/InAs interface to understand the influence of the magnetic EuS layer on the semiconducting InAs electrons. The research employed a combination of density functional theory and Slater-Koster models to analyze the total density of states and electronic framework. The bonding configurations of the Eu/InAs and S/InAs interfaces were also examined to derive magnetic band gaps. According to our calculations, the magnetic band gap of the InAs electrons is highly sensitive to the bonding arrangement at the EuS/InAs interface. This analysis provides insights into the electronic framework and its dependence on the magnetic properties of the EuS layer.

A significant insight from Saint-Raymond and Wadge showed that the Wadge degree of any Borel set in a Polish space either corresponds to a countable number of distinct classifications or all possible classifications are represented. Theorem 4.1 in this text provides a precise condition under which a countable classification occurs, and while it was previously known to be true for Q-space, our result expands the range of applications to an expanded Q-space and other spaces with countable inductions. The article also presents an efficient method to determine the Wadge degree within the countable classifications, specifically applied to Q-space, and demonstrates that the wadge degree of the set of non-periodic reals offers a strong indication of the strength of induction principles.

Highly scalable, custom hardware like Field-Programmable Gate Arrays and specialized computing units such as Tensor Processing Units are effective for accelerating end-of-line training processes. A key benefit is their large storage capacity, which allows them to handle the data and model updates faster than general-purpose CPUs. Pruning has emerged as a way to reduce the size of the machine learning model without significantly impacting its performance, which in turn results in a speedup when using custom hardware as measured by the time it takes for the model to improve during training. Research has shown the potential of FPGAs and TPUs to speed up the training process compared to top-tier CPUs. This study focuses on four approaches to click feedback prediction using FPGAs, which has yielded these outcomes: 1. Single-precision floating-point was initially used but resulted in a 2.4x improvement by switching to 8-bit fixed numbers. 2. We found that 98% of a model can be reduced by using 8-bit fixed numbers. By switching to 16-bit fixed numbers, a further 99% reduction is possible. We observed these benefits using the real-world Great American Clicks (GAC) dataset for a period of 14 days. We noticed that both 8-bit and 16-bit fixed numbers architectures resulted in a faster training process due to their small model size and inputs/outputs, which resulted in a 2.4x and 1.8x improvement respectively

This study expands the modular semantics for non-modal Lambek Calculi into a framework that incorporates both modal operators and order properties. Specifically, we transform the distributive complete Lambek Calculus with tensor and par (DCLP) into a relation-based system that we demonstrate is logically equivalent to a corresponding axiomatic system with modal components. Furthermore, DCLP's semantic foundations enable the development of a complete sound and strong strategy within an inductive sequential proof method framework.

The observation of neutron star-black hole collisions through gravitational waves is expected to offer significant astrophysical insights. The distinctive features of these events, including the black hole mass, allow them to be distinguished from binary neutron star collisions. This study proposes a method to automate the detection and classification of neutron star-black hole collision signals using machine learning, leveraging the effectiveness of convolutional neural networks for image analysis. By applying a similar technique to gravitational wave data, we aim to develop an automated detection and feature extraction system. Our findings indicate that a network with two layers, including 512 and 256 nodes respectively, achieves the highest accuracy of 99.6% in classifying gravitational waves based on simulated LIGO/Virgo data with varying signal-to-noise ratios.

Our analysis of data from the TESS mission yielded a transiting exoplanet, TOI-5542b, with a roughly 3.2-day orbital period and a 99.3% estimated radius relative to its host star, giving it a roughly 1.1 Jupiter radius in size. Using stellar data from three different research groups, we determined the mass of the exoplanet to be approximately 1.07 Jupiter masses. Situated 65.94 parsecs from the solar system, TOI-5542 is a G-type star with an estimated age of about 9 billion years. Previous studies have shown the star to have low metallicity, $[Fe/H]\approx-0.54$, yet TOI-5542 is home to a large, hot Jupiter with a temperature of around 1500 K, characterized by low gravity, which is unusual considering its host star's composition. Notably, our findings include the discovery of a rare gas giant exoplanet with a short orbital period, orbiting a metal-poor G-type star with a age of at least 9 billion years old.

This paper introduces an algorithm to resolve the constrained Markov choice problem, a mathematical optimization issue with wide-ranging applications in economics, operations research, and biology. We adapt the Lagrangian dual function, breaking it down into two components, and then focus on minimizing the first component by leveraging a choice procedure. This method allows us to utilize carrier processes to compute the variational distance between two stochastic models, which we incorporate into the algorithm. We investigate its convergence under two scenarios: when it completes in finite steps and when its runtime is unlimited. Additionally, the proposed algorithm resolves a specific case of the optimal control problem with non-negligible constraints.

This paper presents an innovative offline handwritten mathematical expression recognition system, based on a novel encoding technique and two advanced deep learning architectures, specifically seq2seq learning and CRF. The Encseq2seq and EncCRF systems were evaluated on the cPRTR off-line HNR dataset and demonstrated state-of-the-art performance with the EncCRF model achieving 89% overall recognition accuracy. The performance gap between the models can be attributed to the complexity of some mathematical expressions and the EncCRF model's intrinsic limitations. Additionally, the study highlights the need for larger training datasets and well-annotated databases to推动 further advancements in offline HNR.

A new approach to sheaf cohomology calculation is introduced, drawing inspiration from supersymmetric quantum mechanics. The Riemann-Roch theorem is obtained as a direct application of this method. The approach is further generalized to Hermitian vector bundles with Chern classes determination via an appropriate application of the method.

To analyze the random fluctuations in the interaction process of a complex network, we employed stochastic flow models, utilizing the Fokker-Planck equation and its related results to examine the dynamics of variability. The concepts of Fokker-Planck coefficients and first passage times were leveraged for this purpose. Our analysis focused on two types of networks, one governed by a multiplicative process and the other by an additive regime. As the parameters changed, the first passage times of these two regimes exhibited distinct patterns, leading to different and unpredictable temporal behaviors. These findings highlight the fundamental significance of variability in driving complexity within systems.

Recent advancements in Reinforcement Learning agents, particularly those utilizing the Actor-Critic framework, have been significantly influenced by the integration of differentiable algorithms from External Differential Algorithms (EDAs). Notable examples include Soft Actor-Critic (SAC) and MaxEnt-Policy Optimization (Max-Po), both of which share similarities in exploring state-space environments while optimizing policy effectiveness and evaluation. Building upon this foundation, this paper introduces a novel approach, Hamiltonian Max-Po (HamMax-Po), which integrates Hamiltonian Monte Carlo (HMC) into Max-Po to accelerate exploration and improve value estimation accuracy. Experimental evaluations demonstrate that HamMax-Po surpasses SAC and Max-Po in both exploration efficiency and value assessment precision.

The fundamental axiom for all natural numbers is formulated, introducing key definitions, notations, and essential properties of integers, along with a defined function to calculate the prime $n$th prime $p_n$, which serves to state and provide a proof of the Twin Prime Hypothesis. This hypothesis asserts that for any natural number $A$, there exist two prime numbers with a gap of 2, which fall within the interval $(p_{n-1}, p_n]$, where $p_n$ is the $n$th prime and $n \ge A$. 

A substantial and novel lemma is also presented, which demonstrates that any composite number $b \ge 4$ has at least one prime factor that is less than or equal to its square root. Consequently, the introduction of a particular function enables us to complete a full proof of the Twin Prime Hypothesis. 

It's worth noting that even though the specific function used to prove the hypothesis is suboptimal, it still implies a significant breakthrough in mathematics - specifically, that S. Chowla's conjecture and B. Conrey and D. Iwaniec's conjecture are false. Furthermore, the conditions under which a particular statement holds would indicate the falsity of the strong Goldbach conjecture.

The development of autonomous underwater vehicles (AUVs) has long been impeded by the challenge of underwater navigation. Sonar technology, though effective for immediate distance measurement, often falls short due to its limited depth. In order to achieve immediate sonar blending, we present an innovative sonar-based navigation module for the Immediate Nav manager. This sonar blending module enables the seamless integration of sonar data for short-range distance measurements. In addition, we introduce a method for sonar pose estimation that accurately determines the position of sonar arrays. Our implemented solution has showcased the feasibility of sonar blending and will serve as a foundation for expanding the capabilities of the Immediate Nav manager.

Nereid, one of Neptune's largest moons, exhibits striking variations in albedo across different surface areas. Researchers analyzed the reflectance spectra of Nereid to understand its surface characteristics. Nereid's surface exhibits a low-albedo and highly uniform texture at wavelengths of 0.9-2.4 $\mu$m, which includes a distinct water-ice absorption band at 1.5 $\mu$m and elevated reflectance in the 1.25 and 2.2 $\mu$m regions. These characteristics contrast with other icy bodies and imply a complex composition. Unlike other objects, the water ice on Nereid shows a diminished red color and increased albedo in the visible light spectrum, which may be attributed to the presence of fine-grained crystalline water ice. Further studies on thermal emission suggest that the ice on Nereid is not fully amorphous. To account for these observations while maintaining a high-albedo feature, the water ice on Nereid must be highly reflective and contain minimal amounts of organic material or dark particles. To explain the Al-H2O mass balance on Nereid while accounting for its unique spectral properties and minimizing the Al content, a specific mass ratio of Al to H2O is proposed.

Let $L$ be the set of lower triangular $3 \times 3$ matrices with entries from the field of real numbers. We define a set $P$ of matrices with a specific structure and prove that the points in $P$ satisfy a particular quadratic equation, which represents a projective plane over a specific affine space defined by matrices of a specific structure. Furthermore, there exists a bijection between the points in $P$ and the elements of a specific affine space, demonstrating that the quadratic equation can be reduced to a standard form. Similarly, the elements of a specific set $B$ of matrices with one element equal to one can be in one-to-one correspondence with the elements of a specific projective space.

In a 1987 paper in the Journal of the London Mathematical Society, Pawlikowski demonstrated the validity of two models that contradict eachother with respect to Po\'ncir\'e's theorem. Building on this finding, we demonstrate that the validity of Po\'ncir\'e's theorem cannot be reduced to a more basic level in set theory, specifically as a consequence of axioms. We achieve this by analyzing a particular set of conditions related to Tukey order and regular cardinals. Furthermore, we explore the relationship between the inclusion of certain ideals and Tukey order, specifically focusing on a modified version of the ideal used in the aforementioned models that contradict eachother with respect to Tukey order.

Building on Fudenberg and Levine's (2015) online learning framework, we enhance their optimal "black box" strategy with improved pessimism, allowing for better evaluation of unknown environments. By replacing their close approximations with a value iteration approach capable of handling any Bayesian problem, our results show that agents can achieve better results by slowing down exploration and taking more risks. Additionally, our analysis allows for faster convergence in specific cases and sheds light on the trade-offs between exploration and exploitation in complex decision-making scenarios.

Dualities in category theory serve as useful tools to increase understanding and resolve issues. This module guide demonstrates how to apply fundamental concepts to a range of topics, including Gz-S categories, triangulated categories, and extriangulated categories. A unifying approach across these topics allows us to recover several significant invariants of homological nature, which serve as effective tools for the study of these topics. Specifically, our methods lead to the development of core duality theorems, the construction of δ-functors of exceptional nature, and applications resulting in functors of with support into intrinsic homological invariants. Initially, the guide covers duality concepts in the context of abelian categories, k-linear categories, and triangulated categories. A functor of exceptional nature between triangulated categories enables the demonstration of with support homology equivalences. Subsequently, essential concepts and constructions related to Torsion pairs are explored, which in turn facilitates the definition of Gz-S structures in extriangulated categories. Finally, the guide delves into duality concepts within the realms of relative homological algebra and K-theory.

The E8 lattice is explored by examining its complexification in relation to the lattice of root strings and how it affects the size of the complexified E8 lattice. This increased size signifies the creation of entanglement between E8 lattice elements, leading to quantum contextuality as verified by the Witten-Goldenfeld-Zagier identity. A relevant connection exists with Feit-Tomiyama's work on quantum mechanics based on the Feynman amplitude lattice and how it relates to E8 via complexification. Additionally, knowledge of complexified lattices provides insights into quantum entanglement in higher dimensions across various physical systems such as spin systems and fermionic/bosonic systems.

Research on flat bands has sparked interest in creating new behaviors, including superconductivity that involves multiple particles at once. Our investigation into a specific set of flat bands demonstrates the development of multiple-body superconductivity at a certain density using an order parameter that is nonzero at the Fermi level. This type of superconductivity surpasses the conventional understanding and conventional superconductivity in specific conditions. We also discovered that the order parameter's magnitude rises exponentially with decreasing density in certain conditions. Our results are based on a lattice model and support the possibility of observing this phenomenon in the material RbCd2As2.

We investigate and establish the validity of a generalized version of the Polya theorem for linked groups, which has been proven in the context of countable groups by the first author and T. Naszódy. Alternatively, our result has been extended to countably generated groups by the second author. We have found the essential condition that must be met by the first Betti number for this version of the theorem to hold, have identified the class of groups to which the theorem is applicable in countably generated groups, and have formulated and studied related theorems.

Presence-absence data, characterized by a preponderance of absent values, are frequently encountered in diverse fields, including ecology and genetics. The abundance of relevant data, particularly when sparse patterns anticipate, necessitates a thorough examination of its dimensional composition, particularly its absent and present value components. Given the absence of established models for analyzing such data types, a comparative evaluation of various techniques suitable for uncovering clustering patterns in high-dimensional presence-absence data is warranted. This study undertakes an extensive investigation of different models and methodologies suitable for clustering such data across a diverse range of scenarios. The investigation entailed the development of specific measures for assessing model fit, both in advance of and following adjustment, in addition to exploring various approaches for constructing feature subsets. Ultimately, it is found that although no single method universally prevails, a diversified collection of methods offers the most reliable means of exploring the dimensionality of this unique data type.

In recent years, working with RGB-Saliency models based on deep learning has seen significant advancement, yet they often struggle with situations where the model receives input from multiple channels. To address this limitation, we introduce a unified approach for salient object detection that accommodates both RGB and RGB-D models. This framework leverages a flexible input interface that accepts either color or depth information and utilizes a flexible input interface that accepts either color or depth information and utilizes a adaptive mechanism to efficiently combine features that are information-rich but mutually exclusive. Comprehensive experiments have been conducted on multiple datasets, including SOD, HKU-MAP, and NYU-V2, to validate the effectiveness of our proposed framework. Notably, our framework yields superior performance compared to the existing state-of-the-art methods in effective RGB-saliency detection tasks and approaches performance of SOTA methods in effective RGB-D-saliency detection tasks.

The UM-IU@LING team participated in the SemEval-2019 work on identifying aggressive language on social media by submitting results for four related tasks. We chose to tackle all of these tasks using a combination of BERT and support vector machine models. Our experience revealed that the tasks posed significant challenges, and we struggled to achieve strong results in the training data environment. However, our solution demonstrated improved performance over the baseline in all tasks, yielding Semeval ranks of 26, 27, 26, and 83 for the respective tasks. Notably, we observed discrepancies between our UM-IU rankings and those of the UM teams, particularly in the tasks related to vulnerability to cyber aggression and hostility detection.

This paper explores the fractions formed by dividing symmetrical and antisymmetrical numbers. We have established that the reduced forms of these fractions have a numerator and denominator that are both unique mathematical entities. Specifically, all numbers that can form the reduced denominator are included in the comma of A000209. We have derived a generating function for the number of antisymmetrical numbers relative to a given number and obtained a three-term recurrence for a related sequence. We have also identified the starting numbers of a sequence representing the reduced forms of these fractions, which can be expressed as a function of two prime numbers.

Computed tomography (CT) technology is extensively utilized in various sectors, including medical diagnostics and industrial inspections. These sectors rely heavily on obtaining clear and detailed internal images of objects. A significant limitation of conventional CT scans arises from monochromatic X-rays, which often suffer from data corruption due to polyenergetic sensor noise resulting in artifacts and compromised image quality. To address this issue, we have developed a novel variational reconstruction model that combines sparse reconstruction, material decomposition, and sensor noise reduction within a single framework. Our reconstruction method leverages advanced variables, penalization techniques, and non-negative matrix factorization to achieve this goal. We have successfully applied our model to reconstruct X-ray CT scan images of a mechanical part sensor noisy images under polyenergetic source using a tomographic and a polychromatical x-ray scanner, respectively. Our results have demonstrated the effectiveness of our approach in handling large-scale data and meeting real-time processing requirements, while also showing superior performance in terms of accuracy and precision compared to existing monochromatic and polyenergetic CT reconstruction methods.

Recent advancements in handwritten text recognition have been largely dependent on vast datasets. However, creating such datasets constitutes a labor-intensive and costly process, particularly for languages with numerous scripts or for specialized domains. To address this limitation, researchers have explored methods utilizing data augmentation and pseudo-data creation techniques. Notably, these approaches have focused on languages with character-level data. In contrast, this research delves into composing data augmentation for handwritten text creation, targeting languages with rich morphological compositions like European languages with morpheme-level data. We present a novel method to generate single-shot composatory data from a small dataset of handwritten text records. This approach yields data with enhanced diversity and realism, surpassing traditional augmentation techniques in hand-written text recognition performance. Moreover, our comparison with baseline methodologies reveals significant improvements in accuracy and efficiency, with the resulting data proving suitable for training hand-written text recognition models even for short and varied records. Ultimately, our work showcases the potential of single-shot composatory data augmentation for handwritten text creation and its valuable contributions to MHDATAS and NLP fields.

Utilizing state-of-the-art nuclear data, heavy nuclei models incorporate numerous multi-shell configurations and a vast number of particles, posing significant computational challenges. In this research, we successfully performed fully first-principles calculations for $^{208}$Pb, featuring 1220 neutrons and 120 protons across eight occupied orbits. Our computations included precise estimates of precise operators for nuclear interactions, specifically the nuclear binding energy and twenty-one components of the Pastore matrix, which encompasses mass, radius, neutron-proton mass radius difference, quadrupole moments, and up to sixth-order mass radius differences, all of which are crucial to understanding Pb isotopes' properties. Our predictions for Pb isotopes 'X' showed remarkable agreement with experimental data for Pb-208's precise properties. Our research highlights that fully first-principles calculations for nuclei with many nucleons is now feasible using advanced computational methods and their application can be extended to Pb and Uranium isotopes 'X' across a wide mass range.

Quantum systems exhibiting topological properties share distinct characteristics that set them apart non-topologically. The one-dimensional SSH model serves as a straightforward example to grasp the fundamental features of topological quantum phenomena. We will employ this model to define and discuss key concepts and mathematical calculations associated with topological quantum properties, specifically the edge-state mode shape, energy spectrum, and topological invariant via Chern number or winding number in band-insulating phases as well as the phase transition criterion via the minimum band gap.

This study determines the exact compactness criteria for composition operators between Bergman spaces of certain types of convex domains in $\mathbb{C}^{n}$ and between spaces linked by a non-degenerate analytic disk and a non-surjective analytic function.

We utilized the known structure of supergravity multiplets in AdS$_5\times$S$^5$ to determine the structure of higher loop interactions. A computer-assisted analysis was also performed to verify our model against string theory calculations. A surprising pattern emerged: the differences between these interactions and free theory counterterms can be resolved by modifying only the two-loop structure. This modification leads to the observation that all multi-loop interactions in AdS space are consistent with free theory expectations, a property which we then used to explore the corresponding interactions in other AdS spaces within supergravity.

High-performance computing on Non-Volatile Memory (NVM) devices faces significant hurdles due to inefficient memory management, which in turn limits the adoption of PyTorch and other frameworks in scientific applications and real-time systems. In this research, we introduce DynaSOAr, a memory management solution designed for high-end GPUs, which builds upon the PyTorch framework. DynaSOAr enhances memory management by minimizing memory access delays and optimizing the working set size for each thread, thereby improving concurrency and reducing memory access pressure on the GPU's memory handling unit. DynaSOAr's performance benefits are validated through a series of comprehensive benchmark tests, which demonstrate substantial gains in speedup, reduced memory usage, and increased throughput in machine learning workloads and real-time applications with limited memory capacities. DynaSOAr yields notable gains in CPU-NVM GPU architectures as well, where it boosts throughput by up to 1.72 times and decreases memory usage by as much as 2.56 times in applications such as stock price prediction and image classification.

This study explores minimal standard $U(1)_X$ models derived from a
confining $SU(5) \times U(1)_Y$ model that was initially embedded within $SO(10)$.
The research is primarily focused on the phenomenology of the surviving $U(1)_X$ symmetry.
Each $U(1)_X$ symmetry in the five $U(1)_X$ symmetries arising from the $SO(10)$'s Democratic decomposition is examined in detail.
The analysis reveals that in four of the models, the coupling of the $U(1)_X$ symmetry to the Standard Model fermions is completely determined by its normalization, leaving little room for experimental variation.
Furthermore, it has been found that the $SO(10)$ origin of these models severely limits the possibilities for introducing right-handed neutrinos into the standard $U(1)_X$ models without incorporating additional right-handed neutrinos into the Democratic matrix.
By examining the phenomenological and theoretical requirements of these models, the research then investigates whether they can be theoretically consistent, with the result that all of them fail to meet the necessary criteria for anomaly-free conditions.

A plastic straw filled with pressurized fluid was studied to understand the properties of fluid transport in biological systems, particularly in straw-like plants that use fluid dynamics to move nutrients. By measuring the stress levels in the straw using an image analysis technique and a machine learning-based classifier, the point at which the straw fails under pressure was determined and found to vary depending on the type of fluid involved. Furthermore, models predicting mechanical stress in the straw and its ultimate stress were developed to allow for prediction of pressurized systems, such as those found in plant xylem, failing based on specific mechanical properties without knowledge of its fluid or flow conditions.

The concept of adversarial training over a restricted set of model interpretations has been established as a means to assess the robustness of machine learning models. This idea can be extended to address uncertainty in probabilistic modeling by interpreting the admissible set as a representation of uncertainty. We formalize this extension within a Bayesian framework by leveraging credal analysis to establish rigorous assurances on model strength. Furthermore, we demonstrate the versatility of this Bayesian approach by efficiently calculating admissible sets using graph-based representations of model definitions and by approximating these sets through convex relaxations of different admissibility criteria. These "strength guarantees" provide the ability to quantify the confidence level associated with various performance assessments, including validation and test evaluations, as well as risk estimation. Our approach is tested on a diverse set of probabilistic models representing regulatory guidelines in the pharmaceutical and real estate sectors.

We analyze the case of a lab-frame accelerated superfluid to demonstrate
the occurrence of Bloch oscillations in superfluids. We explain this phenomenon
using a Landau two-fluid description based on the Gross-Pitaevskii equation.
To further clarify, we provide an analogy between this oscillation and the
Kondo effect in semiconductors with a p-n junction. Lastly, we explore the
immediate practical significance of our findings for use with ultracold atoms.

A code that has neighbour symmetry in a specific geometric context is defined as neighbour-transitive in that geometry. A specific type of neighbour-transitive code in a certain geometry is explored. A proven example of such a code is given, namely a binary code that corresponds to a specific geometry called the Wilson quadrangle. Additionally, a classification of neighbour-transitive codes in a specific geometry has been proposed and partially proven. A relationship between neighbour-transitive codes in a specific geometry and a type of design is also established. A theorem relating to an existing code classification has been formulated but requires verification of certain hypotheses.

Investigating the mass distribution within the Central Molecular Zone is a crucial area of research in the context of the Galaxy's formation and evolution. To better understand this complex region, we utilized a sophisticated method corresponding to the 2D correlation function to analyze the anisotropic mass arrangement of the SCUBA-ISO-GALAXY survey. By doing so, we were able to identify a distinct elliptical pattern at large scales, characterized by a significant correlation length of around 180 parsecs and an axis ratio of approximately 1.5. Our findings indicate that the EZM model effectively accounts for the observed EZ pattern to a large extent, contributing significantly to our knowledge of the CMZ's mass arrangement.

By analyzing X-ray absorption edge near-edge spectra taken at high speeds and fast X-ray lasers, we observe significant changes in absorption as material electron shells are populated. To better understand these changes, we created a model that connects population dynamics with the observable shifts in spectra. This intersection of time- and energy-resolved data offers a wealth of information, but our analysis reveals inconsistencies in previously proposed models. To address this, we developed a new framework that accurately predicts absorption edge changes based on the occupation of specific electronic orbitals. This model considers both initial and final states, incorporating matrix elements to represent transitions. By comparing our predictions with experimental data from fast X-ray lasers, we verify its effectiveness and illustrate its application to copper. Ultimately, this framework serves as a bridge between measurable absorption changes and the underlying population dynamics, enabling the interpretation of population dynamics from rapid spectroscopic measurements across various materials.

This paper presents a temperature sensor designed for use across a wide temperature range of -40{\deg}C to 125{\deg}C, capable of achieving 0.24{\deg}C temperature resolution with minimal power consumption. The design employs an adaptive voltage supply and simplified architecture to minimize variance in manufacturing. A novel design feature utilizes the difference in bandgaps between two sub-circuits to provide supply voltage independence, enabling supply voltage ranges from 0.6V to 1.8V. Furthermore, the proposed design incorporates a start-up circuit and demonstrates exceptional performance in both simulation and testing environments. The results demonstrate a maximum temperature measurement error of $\pm$1.4{\deg}C, along with 0.24{\deg}C temperature resolution, along with 1.06nJ energy per conversion at 100kHz supply current, achieved in a 130nm CMOS process.

Quantum entanglement plays a pivotal role in enabling secure communication and precision measurement in quantum physics. A specific form of entanglement, known as polarization entanglement, has been successfully implemented without classical correlation drawbacks in experiments. Here, we outline a method for creating polarized entanglement with guaranteed outcomes, which overcomes the classical limitations and enhances detection efficiency. This method, based on the quantum scissors, utilizes quantum error correction to eliminate mistakes and leverages post-selection in detection. It relies on a single quantum memory with high efficiency, simplifying the system design. With the current best-performing components, our system achieves an overall entanglement rate of 0.01 MHz. A theoretical analysis even explores the implications of detecting single photons in the Bell-state measurement step, and we provide references for achieving fully efficient detection.

A geometric euclidean spanner of a set of points X, denoted as G(X), is given. It preserves distances in X with a multiplicative error factor of at most $\rho$ and adds few edges to the original point set. We define virtual euclidean spanners, which have even fewer edges than G(X), by finding a subset X' of X and creating G(X'). It has a multiplicative error factor of at most $\rho$ and adds few edges to the original point set. We provide an efficient algorithm to find a virtual euclidean spanner of size of O(m$\rho$^O(1)) given X, m edges, and an upper bound on $\rho$. We show that a stronger version of these structures, called radix euclidean spanners, can also be computed in the same time, which have even fewer edges and preserve distances with an additive error factor of zero. We establish a lower bound on the size of these structures, and our results hold in the cell probe model. We present an alternative version of our result, in which the upper bound on $\rho$ can be replaced with the additive error factor of the euclidean spanner. We use a unique approach, adapting ideas from well-known geometric sparsification techniques, to achieve our lower bound.

Accurate categorization of IoT devices via their data packets is essential for network surveillance and intrusion prevention, but current methods neglect the cost of extracting features from the packets. This study aims to provide a practical and cost-effective for traffic analysis by developing a model that determines the optimal depth of TCP packets to examine. Initial experiments using stochastic models revealed that shallow depths of traffic analysis can yield high accuracy, but limited the applicability to specific protocols. However, through extensive experiments across multiple devices and scenarios, we demonstrated that our model works across all analyzed protocols. Building on these findings, we further explored feature sets consisting of packet length and inter-packet time differences, discovering improved performance over existing sets but also increased costs. Ultimately, using our model along with optimized feature sets resulted in better overall performance and lower feature extraction costs, specifically when evaluating traffic at a depth of 5 packets on average.

Godel modal logics can be viewed as extended logical systems that incorporate topological properties into the Godel algebras used to represent them. Research has shown that this class of logics can be fully characterized by specific types of algebras. Building on this finding, recent papers have outlined methods to determine the complete semantics for extended Godel modal logics that involve multiple variables, using alternative semantic frameworks such as valuations in the generalized Kripke style and a new type of algebraic structure that we, in this paper, refer to as relational Godel modal algebras. These papers also demonstrate that the logics can be characterized by specific types of these algebras. To achieve this characterization, these papers introduce two foundational concepts: completeness in the sense of Sahlqvist and the canonical structure of the canonical relation in the canonical algebra. We show that the canonical structure plays a crucial role in determining the relationship between the theorems of the extended modal Godel logics and the specific types of algebras that validate them. Finally, the last section of the paper compares our relational approach to the existing valuations style for Godel modal logics.

This research explores the potential of leveraging external bilingual data to improve real-time word alignment in low-resource languages. It investigates whether bilingual data from a well-resourced, similar language can be utilized to enhance alignment in a less resourced language. Specifically, it was discovered that using an well-resourced language, such as English, can be beneficial even for alignments with a less resourced, geographically similar language, in this case Russian. Additionally, it was found that a model can be refined through the use of bilingual data and subsequent fine-tuning on a less resourced language results in improved performance compared to a model trained solely on the less resourced language. This outcome suggests that leveraging external bilingual data can provide a potential solution for word alignment in languages with limited resources.

This research paper suggests a novel strategy for building Nash equilibria in finite games. It does so by presenting a sequence of games with altered objectives, S_ε for ε > 0, which gradually converge to the original game as ε tends to 0. Each equilibrium in S_ε, known as a distorted best response Nash equilibrium, is characterized by a specific utility trade-off, with players gaining an infinitesimal advantage by deviating from the equilibrium in a specific direction. We prove that any limit point of S_ε as ε tends to 0 results in a Nash equilibrium. Moreover, we find that S_ε has a property where it's always possible to find a solution within a fixed bounded interval for ε's sufficiency. We also establish bounds on how quickly these distorted best response Nash equilibria approach the game's pure strategy Nash equilibria in certain games with specific properties.

The theoretical framework of primordial black holes offers a viable candidate for dark energy due to its proposed formation during cosmic inflation. We utilize the PopSyCLE code to simulate the hypothetical PBH Dark Energy scenario by incorporating new source terms into the Einstein field equations. Our implementation integrates a comprehensive population of Black Hole X-ray binaries (BHXBs) derived from the stellar evolution simulator PopSyCLE, accounting for mass transfer processes that influence binary evolution. Although the PopSyCLE-derived BHXB population lacks the necessary tight orbital periods required for PBH Dark Energy, our results reveal an underlying balance between the mass decrease due to mass transfer and the growth of supermassive black holes through mergers. This finding suggests the necessity of enhancing the PopSyCLE's binary evolution capabilities to accurately model the PBH Dark Energy scenario and assess its potential effects on the universe's evolution.

The geometric characteristics of wedges have significant implications for understanding liquid crystals, where the modulation of the wedge angle gives rise to a variety of unique phase modulations. These phases exhibit both nematic and smectic properties and their existence has been confirmed experimentally. To explore the effect of hard-core interactions on phase behavior, we modelled a system of wedge-shaped particles and observed the phase transitions resulting from changing the wedge angle and attractive forces. We found that increasing the wedge angle leads to various stanzas with different topological features, where the cross-sectional area of the system decreases. Additionally, some of these phases display a zigzag pattern of the stanza interfaces, while others exhibit a more regular structure. Our study also revealed the influence of wedge angle on the smectic layer spacing and the occurrence of defects within the system.

Understanding random fields on a sphere is crucial due to the numerous applications in geography. Despite the significance, the random fields modeling approaches are often underrepresented. Since the derivation is typically complicated, it can be difficult to implement and analyze, particularly when gradients are involved. Researchers have developed and analyzed new Markov One-Step Recurrences for spherical random fields, showcasing how certain geometric properties lead to One-Step decompositions. The applications of these recurrences include the development of marginal distributions and conditional analyses, such as auto-regressive models for spherical fields. The paper provides illustrative examples to demonstrate the concepts and applications.

We have developed a undetector-based, single-pixel measurement tool for observing the behavior of photons in the absence of detection. This home-detect method of measurement offers the biggest advantage in implementing quantum visualization undetected particles while overcoming a major obstacle to achieving it. Consequently, we were capable of implementing quantum correlations, such as two-point spatial coherence and the quantum Fisher function correlation, without detecting photons. Our research further demonstrates the detection-free transfer of image data via two-point spatial coherence and the transfer of high-resolution data via the quantum Fisher function correlation.

The movement of dry liquid foams, which exhibit minimal elasticity, is primarily governed by their internal friction. This frame-independent property has been a subject of study, with the most successful models being those grounded in particle-like behavior. Yet particles experience hydrodynamic interactions that give rise to this predicted behavior, providing a clear understanding of the process. Nonetheless, the nature of the texture in the liquid foam plasma that likely causes this friction, which has been a subject of debate, has not been thoroughly understood. This study employs direct simulations and experiments, which allow for a thorough examination of the plasma's microstructure, linking this friction to phenomena of particle-like interest and explaining its origin through sound.

The availability of high-quality datasets is essential for developing reliable algorithms in medical research and medical image analysis. However, due to an imbalance in the quality of the data available, many training datasets exhibit inconsistencies that can lead to the development of unreliable models. In this study, we explore the application of deep learning and entropy-based feature extraction to not only classify images accurately but also to identify anomalous images that exhibit atypical features. By analyzing and filtering out anomalous images before training, we aim to enhance the quality of the data used and develop more dependable models. The outcome of this research indicates a significant improvement in the accuracy of the results by eliminating irregular images, thereby contributing to the development of a more balanced medical image dataset.

As part of our investigation into the validity of Fermi-liquid theory using numerical simulations, we focused on the sodium element. Our study employed single particle diffusion Monte Carlo to obtain the fully interacting green function and then analyzed its self energy. By examining the temporal decay of the self energy, we were able to determine the quasi particle lifetime. We found that the quasi particle lifetimes align with existing theoretical predictions. Furthermore, we analyzed the self energy across the sodium Brillouin zone and identified its dependence on kinetic energy relative to the Fermi level. Our data revealed that the real part of the self energy is considerably smaller in magnitude compared to the free electron case, while the imaginary part exhibited kinetic energy proportionality, as anticipated by Fermi liquid theory.

In nonlinear physics, the volume variation problem plagues the efficient use of global methods for solving differential equations due to the accumulation of numerical errors leading to volume expansion and solution divergence over long durations. We've developed a technique to overcome this limitation through local transformations that preserve the equation's phase space volume, and we've successfully applied it to global methods如 symplectic mapping for enhanced long-term stability. We've specifically employed a modified expansion process to illustrate the technique's effectiveness in global nonlinear dynamic analysis. We've utilized a symplectic map for a particular case of free expansion in a nonlinear oscillator to demonstrate the phase space volume variation accumulation effect, and we've further explored its implications for a gravitational potential-driven oscillator and a RLC circuit with a fractal capacitor. These examples highlight the importance and versatility of our technique.

This paper provides detailed computations of weights for link curvature graphs in low dimensions ($n = 3, 4$) for general symplectic manifolds with a metric of positive or negative curvature ($K > 0$ or $K < 0$). A general formula is also provided for the weights of link curvature graphs on any manifold $\Sigma$. Furthermore, we establish a crucial link between our findings and the weights of Kontsevich graphs used in Kontsevich's de Rham homotopy algebra and the Kontsevich-Kuperberg-Yoshioka theorem.

We investigate whether high-amplitude, strongly localized modes can persist in low-nonlinearity environments, and have found that the localized modes of the woodpile model and the diatomic array support small levels of energy transfer and saturation via the application of the continuum approximation and the phase-matching principle. This results in the emergence of unique small-coupling localized eigenstates, referred to as nanoptera, composed of an exponential core, oscillating components, and damped corrections. The amplitude of these oscillations depends on the applied external force.

Non-Gaussian patterns in the cosmos' primordial features can be spotted through cosmological observers, and these patterns are linked to a specific type of resonance known as the "cosmological collider effect," which takes place when heavy primordial features appear twice, leading to an exponential signal amplification. Typically, researchers believe this resonance effect can only occur when primordially produced features originate from scales similar to the cosmic horizon during the inflationary period. However, this research demonstrates that the resonance effect can also be witnessed at much smaller scales, where heavy features leave a significantly enhanced signal, and it's possible to detect this phenomenon through a proposed reanalysis of existing data from the primordial background. Moreover, this reward effect isn't exclusively limited to inflationary physics, but can also arise in conformal gravity models like traditional multi-conformal gravity, where a new particle signal may be coupled to the cosmic inflationary signal in an eight-point interaction, yielding a distinguishable $E^6$-dependent amplitude growth pattern, which could be observable if its production rate isn't excessively low.

Graph pairings are established between collections of graphs, specifically mapping the linear arrangement of vertices in a path or cycle to a specific type of accordion graph. The results show that certain variants of the n-hamiltonian wheel are isomorphically equivalent to specific cyclotronic versions of $W_{n,4}$. These findings provide a systematic method for classifying these isomorphisms and have implications for the study of Hamiltonicity and pairings in graphs.

We investigate two types of three-state quantum walks, analyzing the dynamics of their walk states and distribution patterns. An increase in initial entanglement and system size is found to amplify oscillatory patterns and slow down quantum walk evolution. In three-state quantum walks, the spread of particle distribution grows in proportion to the square root of time, matching the dynamics of typical diffusive processes. Moreover, at certain parameter settings, the particle distribution follows a non-Gaussian shape, and in the long term, it converges to a Gaussian distribution. We also observe the emergence of dynamical scaling in the probability amplitudes when adjusting algorithm parameters, and the transition between different evolution regimes and stationary states can be predicted using initial condition-based features.

The self-supervised learning approach of contrastive contrastive learning has proven effective for visual tasks but has been challenging to apply to self-supervised language model training. This difficulty stems from generating accurate transformations of input data and defining relevant property embeddings. To overcome this challenge, a framework is presented that utilizes the Instruct-DAN model to automatically create properties for both visual and text-based inputs, eliminating the need for human input. The framework is then employed to train the vantage-point representation vDAN for cross-modal embedding. The innovation lies in using the Instruct-DAN's optimization process to guide the selection of properties that effectively enhance the quality of the cross-modal embedding. The framework was tested on the benchmark NIST-2M image dataset, achieving superior results compared to existing methods that rely on human-defined properties and even surpassed a supervised baseline in the domain of image classification. The framework is planned to be made publicly available.

A proposed dissipation model in a flat universe is developed to incorporate the combined effect of dark matter and dark energy through a single, combined fluid. By employing a dimensionless coupling coefficient, the dissipation coefficient is expressed and then rewritten in terms of the critical density. Further analysis of the effective equation of state reveals that the condition for stable dissipation corresponds to a specific range between -1 and -1/3. Re-writing the dissipation coefficient as the ratio of two densities reveals that, when assuming conservation of the energy density of dark energy, stable dissipation implies that the combined fluid has a more negative equation of state than -0.5. In contrast, when considering the conservation of dark matter's energy density, the dissipation coefficient assumes a constant value, leading to a simplified analytical solution for the scale factor in terms of the Hubble parameter's power series expansion. This analytical solution enables the calculation of specific values for the dissipation and combined fluid equations of state under two distinct boundary conditions.

A simple, direct proof of a theorem stating the invariance of solution properties under certain transformations was utilized to demonstrate the ill-posedness of incompressible Euler equations when using Sobolev spaces that border on critical levels. This demonstration specifically targets cases involving rough initial conditions. Furthermore, by leveraging the same method, a rapid proof of a strategy-based solution to a problem concerning the incompressible Navier-Stokes equations was also presented.

A prominent denoising diffusion model (DDP) has significantly advanced the field of generative AI by generating high-quality, diverse images, yet bypasising the limitation of uncontrolled generation due to the lack of semantic awareness in the DDP framework. In response, numerous semantic control generation models based on DDP have emerged; however, most are confined to basic tasks such as class-guided, text-guided, and image similarity-guided generation. Unlike these models, we introduce the concept of latent semantic steering in the DDP framework, enabling the precise control of diverse semantic aspects during the image generation process without modifying the original DDP framework. Our approach introduces a semantic awareness module called the Steady Creator in the latent realm, allowing the injection of custom semantic concepts into images and adjusting their intensities. As a result, users can freely and precisely manipulate image attributes including background, object count, color, and style in a continuous, latent, and unidimensional latent realm. Moreover, we also introduce the concept of negative semantic intensity and limiters in our framework, allowing users to exclude unwanted semantic aspects and set boundary conditions for image generation. Extensive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed model, outperforming the current state-of-the-art semantic control generation models and achieving high-quality image generation results with customized semantic aspects, all without modifying the original DDP framework.

Traditional image modification methods often lead to noticeable issues like blooming artifacts and decreased quality when trying to hide information in images. Research into alternative approaches has emerged, with the Bayesian Neural Network (BNN) being one such innovation. Building upon the foundation of 2x DOBI, a previous 1x quality-reverse method was a step in this direction. Our work takes this further by integrating 2x DOBI with BNNs to create a highly effective, quality-reverse image steganographic technique. We introduce a novel block-based approach coupled with an enhanced filter system to handle the blooming artifact problem, utilizing a new type of horizontal and diagonal filter crafted with the support of an optimization strategy. By applying these techniques, our method results in a considerable improvement in image quality and embedding capacity compared to 2x DOBI and BNN alone. Our findings demonstrate that the proposed BNN-based method outperforms existing high-quality image steganographic techniques while maintaining a high secret image mean squared error (MS-E) within an acceptable range.

Our investigation focuses on the possibilities that neutrinos interact weakly with each other through Higgs-related forces or that they couple to dark energy through gravitational effects, ultimately leading to neutral-neutral portals being opened. In a search for evidence of these interactions, we examine the significance of the $J/\psi$ decay into a photon and invisible matter on one hand, and its completely invisible counterpart on the other. In contrast to the photoinvisible channel, the invisible channel is heavily restricted by current data. As a result, our most sensitive measurement comes from combining a various set of restrictions on one hand the lovelock coefficient and Cherenkov-like mode conversion of neutrinos, and on the other hand Fermi's constant and neutrino self-interaction effects in beta decay processes.

The traditional solar magnetic bright spot phenomenon has persisted for over four decades in solar physics research, yet its definition has remained elusive. Our 21-year analysis of solar magnetic bright spots near the sun's central meridian, derived from SOHO/LASCO images, reveals evidence for two distinct populations. These populations exhibit different characteristics in terms of magnetic field strength, field complexity, brightness, and location, aligning with the magnetic field properties observed at the sun's surface and those detected within the corona, respectively.

In our investigation, we explore the use of very short human movement data, known as minimal clips, for identifying D-Learner models. These short clips present challenges due to the lack of context, potentially leading to poor performance in dynamic identification. To overcome this issue, we propose a new approach that utilizes a comprehensive dataset of full-body videos of individuals performing the same action, from which we generate synthetic short clips that match the content of the available human data. By training our model on this simulated data, we enhance its ability to generalize and achieve better results compared to previous methods.

If certain assumptions hold, galactic magnetic fields should have collapsed with the galactic disk. However, they've survived up to the present day, suggesting a possible explanation. This could be attributed to dark matter taking the form of magnetic monopoles that resist the galactic compression. This dark matter scenario, assuming the existence of milli-magnetic monopoles, is explored in detail. As monopoles in the galactic disk encounter external forces, they segregate based on polarity due to the field's orientation, leading to an imbalance in the antimonopole-to-monopole ratio. The overall effect is that one type of monopole neutralizes the other, leaving a negligible amount of the dominant type, which is consistent with current experimental limits. The surviving monopoles exert a continuous weak pressure on the galactic disk, helping to preserve the long-lived magnetic fields we observe today. The monopoles could be thought of as the dark matter in U(1) magnetic charge models, which could be generated through processes like Grand Unification symmetry breakdown, making them a potential candidate for dark matter.

Extreme weather events pose significant threats to the environment and economy, making the accurate forecasting of temporal patterns in climate data a crucial area of study. Due to the vast amounts of data involved, traditional models are often impractical, leading researchers to turn to more modern approaches. However, the limitations of these models in terms of interpretability and performance consistency remain significant challenges. This research addresses these issues by proposing a new model, U-SWVC-Encoder, based on the transformer architecture, which is specifically designed to work efficiently on large-scale climate data. The novel model incorporates a window-based cross-attention approach to maintain long-term patterns, while also introducing a novel encoder that reduces the computational burden. Furthermore, a new analysis framework is developed to assess the models' fidelity and reliability, which sheds light on their capabilities in terms of prediction and interpretability. A comprehensive comparison with existing models demonstrates the superiority of the proposed model in terms of accuracy and scalability, and the results indicate that the proposed model outperforms its counterparts in terms of both accuracy and runtime efficiency.

A newly proposed model with $S_3$ symmetry and VACUUM stability is analyzed,
identifying multiple possible arrangements for dark matter within the $V_4$ potential,
each containing two scalar fields that can contribute to dark matter,
resulting in five distinct but theoretically feasible models,
these models exhibit varying degrees of vacuum stability,
stability can be reassessed through the correction terms due to loops,
finally, some key observational search strategies are introduced as starting points.

The PPT quadrilateral hypothesis (PPT4) posits that the set of low-rank PPT states and the set of low-rank NT states are separately closed under the action of local unitary transformations. PPT4 has been validated for specific scenarios, such as two-qubit and qutrit-biqudit systems, but its general validity remains unconfirmed. PPT4's validity would facilitate the classification of PPT states and the quantification of quantum correlations via entanglement. A new hypothesis (H4) is introduced, suggesting the density of PPT states and NT states within low-rank density matrices is zero. PPT4 and H4 are contradictory, yet PPT4 is preferable as it enables the classification of states and practical applications. PPT4 is confirmed for low-rank states involving up to seven qubits under specific conditions.

Neural traffic jams could be the underlying cause of neurodegenerative disorders. To investigate ion transport congestion in axons, a control problem was formulated where the ion pump rate control was optimized. In axons, K+-ATPase and Na+-K+-ATPase ion pumps balance the intracellular and extracellular concentrations of Na+, K+, and Cl- ions. Due to K+ congestion in axons, the efficiency of these pumps diminishes, requiring higher ATP to maintain ion balance. Through the derivation of a new system of partial differential equations, the work demonstrates that optimal ion pump regulation is feasible, yet in the absence of axonal traffic, optimal regulation offers minimal energy savings compared to optimal regulation.

The analysis of complex systems like financial data often benefits from the application of network science. This research demonstrates the feasibility of finishing in asset correlation networks by exploring the prevalence of network motifs which provide valuable insights into the network's overall structure and stability. Our results reveal that filtering data noise significantly improves the accuracy of correlation network analysis, allowing the network size and the number of network nodes to provide relevant information about the market's health. Moreover, the stability of the network can be evaluated by comparing the observed network motif occurrence with their expected counts, which provides a stronger basis for research and more reliable forecasting than traditional financial metrics.

As a star collapses into a black hole, it passes through the innermost stable orbit at a critical point, where it emits intense radiation. Since the star is much smaller than the black hole, it doesn't form an accretion disk. Instead, we use a numerical method to simulate the intense emissions generated during this unique event. As the star spirals inward, it breaks apart into tiny particles, releasing a massive amount of energy in the form of light. Our simulations show that the brightest flash can last only a few milliseconds, while the overall event can last up to several minutes. These intense emissions can be seen across a wide range of frequencies, from X-rays to microwaves. Notably, the peak frequency can be as high as the gigahertz range, depending on the size of the black hole. When the star reaches its final descent, it gets trapped in a rapid spin around the black hole, releasing even more intense radiation before ultimately being swallowed whole.

In τ lepton decays involving three bodies, secondary baryons are produced; however, their rates are significantly lower compared to other outcomes due to the high mass barrier. To better understand the relevant processes, a theoretical framework was developed: a three-body formalism was created to calculate the secondary baryon production rates, taking into account the complex interaction between the particles. As input for this model, form factors were obtained by applying the light-con sum rules method, specifically for the interaction between a pion and either a neutron or a lambda baryon as part of the final state. Notably, the interaction between the pion, neutron, and proton was found to be negligible in comparison. Our predictions indicate a 1.1% probability for τ → K^- p n ν_τ and a 0.6% probability for τ → K^- Λ p ν_τ. These results suggest the potential for τ decay to serve as an experimental testing ground for verifying the light-con sum rules predictions.

The para-Jaccard distance family is defined by the parameterized function d_(α,β) (A,B) = (α|A specifically not in B| + β|B exclusively not in A|) / (αβ + β|B exclusively not in A| + α|A specifically not in B| + αβ), where the sets involved in A and B are defined as follows: elements present solely in A as (A specifically not in B) = (A minus the intersection of A and B) and elements present solely in B as (B exclusively not in A) = (B minus the intersection of A and B). The study identifies the conditions under which d_(α,β) satisfies the requirements for a valid distance measure, specifically that it results in a value less than one and satisfies the symmetry requirement. When α = β = 1, a unique scenario arises resulting in the well-known Jaccard distance; however, the analysis shows that setting extreme values of the (α,β) pair results in interesting and comparable behavior, resembling the relationship between the Jaccard distance and the normalized information distance. This leads to a proposed parametrized group of distances that bridges the gaps between these two different distance concepts.

Achieving clear images from motion-blurred photographs is a highly desired goal, 
as it enables access to high-quality images even in the presence of movement 
blur. Nevertheless, current methods are limited due to the challenges in 
reconstructing clearest possible images when human subjects are involved and 
unknown movement blur. In this research, a proposed model utilizes peroxide 
permutation and residual learning to generate an input image that is blurred 
by estimated blur parameters in order to refine the recovery process. The 
estimated parameters include the magnitude and direction of movement, the 
time duration, and per-frame residual features that enhance the complex 
image restoration task. The results show the efficacy of the method on 
synthetic and real-world images with significant improvements in visual 
quality, as evidenced by the calculated PSNR, SSIM, and LPIPS values.

Our innovative approach leverages the unique properties of aromatic molecular frameworks, specifically their electron-activated redox responses, to create a functional neuron model. We've successfully designed a computational neuron framework using the [Fe(py)2L]2+ framework, where one pyridine ligand is replaced by a ferrocene redox mediator and the other by a diaminobenzene unit. When an electrical stimulus is applied, reducing the ferrocene within the framework triggers the growth of an electroactive radical cation. This results in the deposition of an insulating material on the framework's surface and reduces its conductivity, effectively mimicking a neuron's membrane potential and synaptic transmission processes. Furthermore, through repeated stimulation cycles, our [Fe(py)2L]2+ framework exhibits increasing insulator conversion rates, replicating the phenomenon of long-term potentiation in biological neurons. Therefore, this molecular framework's behavior exhibits a fundamental computational capability to represent the fundamental electrical processes of biological neurons.

A specific type of set up, known as a well-ordered set, allows for the creation of an ultrapower structure that's particularly useful in understanding mathematical concepts. In this paper, the authors establish the existence of ultrafilters that enable the creation of complete ultrapowers, which in turn, have the desirable property of being homogeneous. Additionally, the authors provide characterization criteria for the embedded order within the ultrapower in terms of special sequences called interval sequences. They also demonstrate that the embedded order is strictly smaller than the original order unless the set has countable cardinality.

The efficacy of various training strategies and algorithmic profiles has been extensively examined in literature. In contrast, significantly less attention is given to characterizing distinct features of particular datasets. Despite numerous profiled approaches exist, each tailored to specific types of problems, there is a notable absence of datasets uniquely identified features being defined. In response, we introduce a systematic method for establishing the unique profile of a dataset. Initially, we identify four categories of unique characteristics in datasets, followed by a proposed pipeline that facilitates empirical validation of these characteristics. Lastly, we highlight understanding a dataset's profile as a prerequisite for evaluating training methodologies and developing algorithmic strategies.

A graph can be made into a complete chromatic product by adding edges based on the colors of adjacent vertices. Researchers strengthened a concept of a graph being chromatically defined and proved that if a graph has a specific number of vertices and is defined by its color classes, then its chromatic number and the number of its cliques have a linear relationship. This result reinforced a Hadwiger conjecture for graphs with a chromatic number of four or five. Researchers then explored whether the defined, chromatically increased graphs have a positive minimum density for three-dimensional networks and provided a partial answer for five-dimensional networks based on recent findings about the circular chromatic number. Researchers also proved that the defined, chromatically increased graphs have a minimum density for three-dimensional networks and were related to the minimum density problem first introduced by Tuza. Researchers also studied how the defined, chromatically increased graphs relate to another graph class introduced by Amini et al. and found relationships between their density problems.

This paper presents a novel technique for restoring smooth graph signals using a modified correntropy approach. We propose an adaptive Generalized Correntropy-Induced Distance (GCI-Distance) approach that effectively minimizes the error between the observed and filtered graph signals, taking into account the non-stationary nature of the distortion. Our method also addresses the uncertainty inherent in the data. We demonstrate that the optimal kernel parameter can be determined without making assumptions about the system. Experiments on synthetic and real-world data sets confirm the effectiveness of our method. We further substantiate its reliability through theoretical analysis.

We introduce a theory for producing quantum interference patterns involving atom interferometers based on spinor systems. By enciphering phase information within the complex quantum state of these interferometers, we exploit the full range of available quantum statistical properties for enhancing sensitivity in measurements. To optimize the state of spinor systems for maximizing sensitivity in detecting noise during interferometric readings, we apply the logarithmic average distance metric, which we utilize to analyze the effect of entanglement within these systems. Furthermore, our model accounts for phenomena like spin precession and loss of coherence, allowing us to utilize undepolarized Moshinsky states to utilize the complete state space and provide an exceptional sensitivity in detecting noise beyond the standard quantum limit.

This research offers accurate estimates for the lowest eigenvalue of a nonlinear elliptic problem that incorporates a Robin boundary condition. Specifically, we provide a nontrivial upper bound that approaches the actual value in the limit of large values, particularly for problems set within domains of expanded size combined with high exponent values for the underlying $p$-Laplacian problem. Above a certain threshold, we also establish a precise estimate for this eigenvalue in the case of large $p$-values.

Graph Convolutional Neural Networks (GCNNs) are a fundamental tool for processing graph-structured data. The basis of GCNNs involves graph convolution, a method used to extract features from graph data. The graph convolutional layer in GCNNs functions by incorporating parameters within filters to capture essential information from the input data. Within the context of GCNNs, matched filters are employed in two distinct ways: pre-trained filters developed from extensive datasets and filters that are automatically generated during training. Pre-trained matched filters have been utilized to enhance the performance of GCNNs in node classification and semi-supervised node classification, whereas GCNNs optimized by matched filters in this study have two distinct advantages: reduced depth of GCNNs and lower overall number of parameters in the model. Additionally, the investigation delves into the implications of using GCNNs with or without matched filters in terms of data smoothness across the input graph. The study provides a thorough analysis of the fundamental operations in GCNNs and makes available GCNNs that are automatically optimized by matched filters under an open-source, reproducible framework.

The rise of generative AI has led to a significant number of AI-generated content online, resulting in a dependency on large, well-documented datasets for identifying AI-generated text. However, the development of specialized models for dependency analysis has required vast amounts of labeled data, incurring high costs for annotation and compromising diversity in languages and writers. To address this issue, we propose a novel framework called DUAL that leverages the capabilities of large AI-generated text classifiers to train low-resource models for dependency analysis, preserving data diversity. Thorough experiments are conducted to verify the efficacy and efficiency of the proposed framework.

This study employs the self-consistent light-front quark model to investigate the $B\to D\ell\nu_\ell$ transition form factors. Utilizing consistent light-front quark model calculations for both $B\to D$ and $D\to \Phi$ transition form factors, we derive the $B\to D$ form factors by applying the quark-meson dominance model, ensuring light-front quark model consistency. Our results yarmouth-date the form factors and the ratio of their conservation and breaking currents, which are compatible with existing lattice QCD and light-front quark model data. We find that the $b\to d$ axial current, $\frac{F_2(q^2)}{m_B+m_D}$, is the most sensitive to $m_c$. Consequently, we use this dependency to predict the $B_c\to D_s$ form factors and present our findings for the decay $B_c\to D_s\ell\nu_\ell$, specifically calculating a decay rate and the forward-backward asymmetry as functions of the momentum transfer squared. This prediction may contribute to resolving the $b\to c$ semileptonic form factor anomaly.

In this research, we explore the relationship between the dimensions of projective spaces and a specific group of transformations known as O(n,R). We demonstrate that the group O(n+1,R) is minimally non-reversible when applied to the transition from the projective space P(n,R) to the next higher dimensional one, P(n+1,R). Furthermore, we define a particular relationship, called a membrane, between two such transitions and examine the impact of a particular subgroup on this membrane. Our research concludes with the mapping of a universal object representing these membranes to the space P(P(O(n,R), O(n,R)^*).

The computational power of LOPTIME, a restricted model of uniform polynomial time computation, has been the focus of extensive study within complexity theory. Despite numerical evidence to the contrary, it remains an unproven hypothesis that P equals LOPTIME. In keeping with this line of investigation, we examine the computational capabilities of uniform models when given graphs as input. Specifically, we show that the computational models P, NP, BPP, P/poly, and BPP/poly all contain a strict superclass within the uniform variant of LOPTIME. This finding holds true for any infinite family of graphs, including those that can be solved in polynomial time by a Turing machine. Moreover, our analysis encompasses the full computational power of LOPTIME with unbounded oracle access and demonstrates two distinct graph families that exhibit this property. The first family consists of weighted networks derived from Cayley graphs, where we prove a polynomial-time solvability. The second family includes the unweighted Cai-Furer-Immerman graphs. Additionally, our research highlights the significance of a looser equality between P and LOPTIME when considering non-uniform computation with graph input, specifically that P equals LOPTIME/poly is equivalent to P/poly equaling LOPP/poly, where the latter denotes the class of problems solvable by an LOPPIME machine with polynomial length advice.

Research has shown that substituting Bi for Eu in the pyrochlore iridate compound (EuBi)2Ir2O7 results in a transition from insulating to metallic behavior. By examining the x-ray emission spectrum of the 5d state of Bi and 5d state contributions to the optical and x-ray emission spectra, we found evidence for insulator-to-metal transitions at various x values. This contribution was found to be significant for 0.75 ≤ x ≤ 1, but not beyond x = 1, indicating that insulator-to-metal transitions occur at two separate compositions within the series. Contrary to expectations, our results do not show any coherence loss in the 5d optical conductivity, nor do they reveal signatures of strong electron correlation at x = 1 in the ferromagnetic compound.
